author: @jules8717
text:
I'm 16, I've been telling stories for as long as I can remember, and I started putting them to paper three years ago. I've always been a "gifted" child--I excelled in math and science, and everyone told me how important and special I was because of my academic achievements, so I thought that my passion for writing was unimportant. I hid it. Even my parents and many of my closest friends had no idea I would pour hours and hours into my stories weekly, or even daily. This year, though, I took a high school writing class, which accompanied my English class. My teacher not only writes but is also very well-respected in the theater community, and has written several original pieces. It was only recently that I had the opportunity to write something creative for his class--a script for an original scene--and by the time I got around to it, I was exhausted from all of my academic work. I wrote the script in under two hours. It was far from my best work, but I simply didn't have the extra time to put into it. After I turned it in, my writing teacher approached me and told me it was outstanding, that he wished he'd had the opportunity to read my creative writing earlier, and that he wanted me to polish it and enter it in a short play contest next year. I'd hidden my love of writing for three years, and almost nobody had ever read, let alone praised, my work, so I was blown away--and I still am. I never dreamed that my "hobby" could be worth acknowledging, but now I was finally being told it was--not by the school system, but by a man who worked in a creative field. In the past few weeks I've opened up more and let more and more people read my work, again, outside of the school curriculum, and I've been told time and time again that I have a promising future in creative writing, if I choose to take it. I've been offered advice, I've been called a prodigy, people have offered to mentor me--it's astounding. And nothing I've shown people has been my best work! But I still have a hard time wrapping my mind around the idea that my creative achievements are more important than my academic ones...because only academic achievement is praised by the school system. I still have to sacrifice most of my time to math and science, because in the eyes of the school system, my writing is not worth a grade. In the eyes of the school system, my passion, my devotion to a creative outlet, means nothing.
I'm not the only person I know in this situation--my experience might be somewhat of an extreme case, but I know gifted artists and musicians who are also seeing their talent and creativity squandered by the school system. I've seen it at every school I've ever been to, with dozens and dozens of passionate people. I've witnessed the exact moment when people gave up on their dreams because they were told math and science were more important than what they loved. The school system kills creativity.

author: @JeffFieldsMcCormack
text:
This was really powerful, and very true. Schooling was created to prepare kids for industrial jobs. This began in the industrial revolution, when many more workers were needed. Creativity and skills were not required. They just needed someone who could drill a hole, set a pipe, calculate the angle, construct the train's engine, etc. Our grades are even modeled after grades of work or meat.
School needs to update. It is in the process of changing and updating, but we should spend more focus on skills, and less on numbers and facts. Yes, we all need to learn these facts, but we also need to hone our intellectual skills. This is what UIL tries to do with their competitions. They try to take the skills that students already have, (writing in my case), and help the students succeed in that field, or with that skill, by putting them against others with similar skills.

text: I'm 16 years old and right now, I hate school. That doesn't sound particularly impactful coming from a 16 year old I know. All teenagers hate school. Everyone knows this. I think that if this is the case, there is something fundamentally flawed in the system. If teachers were allowed to teach however they wished, I honestly believe that schools would be better. Teachers are generally very conscientious people, they want to help students succeed and they know the best way to help each student but having their job hanging on their compliance with rigid and arbitrary standards set by people who have never taught in their lives is an absurd situation. It's akin to if the paralympic games didn't categorise the disabilities and told an amputee to swim the same race as a blind man. People are different, so the ways in which they do things should be allowed to be different as well. Just a few thoughts of mine.

author: @Cosmalano
text:
One of the biggest things I took out of it was
that I felt like he was trying to get across the point that everyone is
creative, but you’re not allowed to be creative in academics. He made the point
that schools prepare children to be college professors RATHER than to help them
be creative, as though a professor must be exempt from being able to have
original ideas. He also made the joke that during a social interaction,
academics are praying for it to end so that they can “go write a paper about it,”
as if to devalue talking about things in a structured way as a viable outlet of
expression. All throughout school, I was one of the few kids that valued
academics above everything else. When somebody asked me, “what’s your hobby?”
and I responded “doing math or learning about physics” people would respond,
“but what do you like to do for fun?” I’d have to give the answer “I play the
piano” instead because it’s a more acceptable answer as a leisure activity. But
I could do math the way a “normal” person my age played sports or played video
games. I could sit down and solve problem after problem for hours, or rearrange
problems and make my own in order to give myself a better understanding of a
mathematical concept. And then I could apply that concept to a physical
situation to find links between things in the real world that I never would
have realized otherwise. I don’t consider myself good at either math or
physics. Were I to ever achieve great success in the fields I would not want my
achievements to precede me the same way high achievers in the arts often seem
to. I would not want my achievements to precede me because I believe that I am
not good at the topics, I merely enjoy them, and I wouldn’t want someone to
feel like I was better than them just because I enjoyed something they didn’t.
Most, if not all people can do math faster than me. I am extremely slow at
doing my work, and for most of my life I felt like that was supposed to mean
that I wasn’t good at it. Eventually, I even grew to hate mathematics. However, at the height of my loathing in the 10th grade, I discovered that if
I tried hard enough, I could comprehend graduate level texts. I was impressed
with myself for this, and unlike the other things in life that I had wanted to
be good at in order to impress others (which admittedly is why I started doing
more complicated mathematics at first), I could do something that I myself
could be proud of, and I realized that was all that mattered. I derived great
joy from discovering new ideas and the ways they link together, or finding my
own new ways to understand something. I have even been brought to tears by the
beauty I find in mathematics, as silly as that may sound. I would even argue,
physics and mathematics are fields that praise creative individuals, as some of
the most notable physicists in history include the likes of Albert Einstein and
Richard Feynman, two men who revolutionized physics by working on ideas that
everyone had worked on before, but in entirely new ways. So, I'd that no, he is wrong. Schools could certainly be reworked to be more inclusive of children that like to do things like dance, sing, paint, etc., or just be more accepting of students that enjoy different
things and learn in different ways in general, but for some, the academic areas
in school are the places THEY get to show off their creativity, and in a world
that continues to attempt to be more inclusive of those we think are being
ignored, we must refrain ourselves from putting the kids we commonly see as
“uncreative” or “creative in the wrong ways” on the back burner, in favor of
those that we think are being ignored.

From K-12, students interact primarily with people of the exact same age, experiences, knowledge and skills, yet they're supposed to function properly in the real world?

author: @upiyinr8413
text:
Do schools kill creativity? | Sir Ken Robinson 
 Throughout the speech, Sir Ken Robinson mainly discusses that schools suppress children's creativity. Schools today tend to treat mistakes as an unforgivable fault, as we can see teachers who go furious when we choose the wrong answer by mistake. Mistakes don't precisely signify creativity, but most revolutionary advances have derived from creative ideas thought to be a 'mistake' in that society. As schools make children fear making mistakes, they grow up to lose the ability to create something inventive and ingenious. Moreover, this phenomenon is occurring throughout the whole world. Schools kill children's creativity not only by prohibiting mistakes but by underestimating subjects regarding creativity so as art and dance. The speaker claims that this phenomenon occurs throughout the whole world since most countries consider the ultimate goal of public education is training professors, which requires not creativity but logic. Likewise, creativity is underrated since it is not essential in industrialized society. What jobs require defines people's value. Artists and musicians make less money, so they are less needed. Following society's common demand of intelligence, university naturally changed into the job training center. The presenter strongly argues that this view on education should be viewed differently. For example, ADHD is defined as an attention disorder, yet if we change our attitude toward it, we can find that people with ADHD are talented in bodily activities such as dancing. In conclusion, the author asserts that humans' future depends on whether they adjust their new concept of the education system which can lead to the flourishing of humanity.
 Even if the presentation was taken more than ten years ago, his idea is determined to be true. Also, the problem he mentioned is still not settled in Korea. What estimates people's value is the university and the specialty they majored in. Korea has not adapted to the fourth industrial revolution, concerned with computing technology that needs creativity. Exams in schools are taken not to give students motivation to study but to exclude them from success. Students in Korea are not "studying" but "memorizing" technical terms that they never understand. How could they make software and A.I.s though they have never created something new throughout their whole life? It is essential to reconsider the nature of the study.

text: Sometimes it's necessary to remember that the way we see the world is often a reflection of how we feel about ourselves. Ultimately, learning to accept ourselves with all our flaws is what allows us to stop seeing limitations where others see opportunities to start over. This ability to transform our personal story is what truly allows us to heal; it's not about ignoring what hurts, but about ceasing to see ourselves through the lens of our shortcomings. Being emotionally well doesn't mean we don't have scars, but rather that we've learned not to let those scars dictate who we are. I used to not get why he hated the dog at first, but now I do.

I have a disability, and whenever someone tries to make you feel included or not alone, it makes you feel weird or different. After I was diagnosed, my horse instructor put me on a horse with similar issues like heat intolerance and all that, and I hated it so much.

It’s the fact that you aren’t normal, and when people remind you, even if they try and make you feel not alone, it’s this constant reminder you’re  different, and people notice and think about that.

It starts to consume you...

So don’t be like “why did he hate the dog! That’s a hypocritical and selfish!” Because you most likely don’t understand

author: @larryisntmynamebutyoucanca9625
text:
After... recent events... I am starting to see so much clearer how the news is all a lie-machine, meant to spoon-feed outrage to people to boost ratings and increase ad revenue. After Kirk got assassinated, my Dad (who only watches Fox) told me "that is the difference between the left", totally regurgitating some ideology that the "opposing side" is inherently more violent. Some of my left-wing friends were outright celebrating, ignoring the fact that someone expressing their First Amendment right was assassinated for expressing their (however polarizing) beliefs.

It feels like nobody sees what is happening. The media we are consuming is totally turning us against each other. Nobody has any sympathy for the "other side", or even their own side, anymore. We are more willing to hurt ourselves to hurt each other than we are to band together to build a stronger society. And this is COMPLETELY BY DESIGN. 

I am at a point where I don't even believe there IS a right or left anymore, because people are not binary. I live in a place where we have trans and gay people that are broadly accepted, yet many of those trans and gay people own and love guns. Many of them go to the rodeo and listen to country music. Does that make them right or left? I know they would pick a side, because are told they should, but in reality, almost all people dont fall cleanly in line with either "side", so is it even a good measurement of people's politics? 

I think the media and the politicians curate this mindset because it drives up viewership and keeps people in line. It keeps us fighting each other so we dont band together and take the rich and poweful elites who sold out our country head-on. It's not even a conspiracy theory. It's textbook history, population manipulation and it has happened in countless places across millenia. We are so focused on fighting a losing, meaningless battle over our own perceived virtue that we aren't even talking about how the elites are stealing everything from under us and lighting a match on their way out the door before they lock us inside. 

The news hates you. The president hates you. The politicians hate you. They think, whoever you are, that you are ignorant peasants, and they treat all of us as such. They hate it when we get along. They hate when you have a good day. They hate it when they can't sell you something so they can fill their neverending money lust. 

I am sick of this. How far are we willing to take things before we realize this is all by design? How many people will die? How many of our liberties will we sacrifice? Calm the hell down and look at WHO is truly telling you to be angry.

author: @Krombopulos
text:
I understand what you’re trying to say, but in troubling times your video comes off as irresponsible and disingenuous. You say to “have faith that times will get better” but better by who? Things only improve when people put in the effort to make change happen.

If you tell people to tune out of what’s going on around them, they could wake up one day to find that many of their civil rights have already been taken away. What do you say to that? Right now, we have someone in power who is actively working to erode the checks and balances of our country. If people don’t become conscious of the forces at play, we risk sliding into dictatorship.

This isn’t the time to tell people to tune out. The responsible thing is to point them toward reliable sources, so they can stay informed without being consumed by negativity. Yes, the world feels heavy and depressing right now, I feel it too, but that’s not a reason to run off and hide. If things were good, we’d all be enjoying them. When they’re not, it means we have to engage, not escape.

Things don’t just miraculously get better. It takes faith, yes, but also willpower and action. That combination is what leads us to a better future. 🙏🏾

text:
My 16 year old daughter and I were in my car, as i was taking her home from work.  We were talking about the past week's news, and it's implications.  She and I are not diametrically opposed in viewpoints, but I am aware of the narratives that target her (and simultaneously the ones that target me).

As we were talking, the highway bottlenecked and came to a stop... we saw the aftermath of a gruesome accident, and everything changed...

She kept saying "I hope they're ok", but I couldn't help but know that no... they were not, indeed.

This past week has changed me.  In the wake of a big event, I chose to shut most of my usual sources out.  ...I already know what most of my usual sources were going to say, and I didn't need to hear it.  Brief headlines are all I need now.  
As much as my dream is simply to become a hermit in the woods, I should at least know the headlines... but it's not worth wholly immersing myself into, as I have a job to do, and children to raise.  Awareness and being informed are important, but the here and now is most important.

author: @guidinglight-
text:
Single most important and resonating video I’ve watched this year. For the past three years, I’ve been following the news regularly, terrible headlines every day: someone killed, someone raped, another financial crisis, government corruption, AI will destroy us, wars. At some point, I realized every channel bends the news to fit its ideology or agenda. I kept watching, just to see how they twist it and how low they can go.

But it became a habit. And with it, anxiety, restlessness, and agitation slowly crept into my life.

This video feels like a godsend. I knew everything you said, but I think I needed to hear it the way you put it together. Thank you.

I’ve unsubscribed from all news channels and pages on YouTube and Instagram, deleted a few news apps, and removed Twitter. Believe it or not, it’s only been a day, and I already feel more peaceful.

author: @YouKnowMyNameLUTN
text:
Thank you.
People don’t realize how the “news” won’t report how people help out each other. They won’t say breaking news a kid helps out an elder man. They don’t realize that they need clicks because in the end, it’s a business in the end no matter what agenda they have they need news in order to profit and no news is gonna be interesting if it doesn’t spike the general public’s interest.
You know how you build a better world? by not trying to fix the world at once when everybody focuses on their environment and try to make it better, that’s when the world as a whole heals. It doesn’t need some big act of revolution like the news makes it out to be.
Most days are mundane, most days were around the same people, and none of the political state of the world actually contributes to the emotions we feel in our regular lives. Everywhere, people feel love, fear, hate, passion, sadness.
Also, do you really think what the news reports is going on is actually what’s going on? If so, how come nothing changes ever? It’s so naive. Powerful people will never actually reveal their true agendas, and what actually is going on.
It’s easiest to sell a narrative and make people fixated on it as the ultimate truth, as it inevitably will divide people endlessly, so they profit off it and distract the general public as a whole.
The day I deleted social media and stopped taking the news so seriously, along with unfriending my friends since I was at middle school as they got me so fixated on the news; that’s the day I actually started to feel life again and stopped feeling so damned.
If everyone can just be kind to their own community, you get a better world. A million people looking to change the world at once will never do anything other than divide the world more and more.

author: @cstone3178
text:
Glad to have you back! And, YES!!! I have been feeling for a long time, that journalism skews more and more to sensationalism. I chalk it up to 1) news no longer being considered a service to the general public but a revenue potential and 2)  the big bugaboo social media engendering in us insatiable appetites for „content“. I am an older Gen Xer and I have watched news divisions on TV, newspapers, and radio news all turn sensationalist AND opinionated. It used to be that a journalist/reporter just reported the news; now they feel free to throw their own personal opinion in as well … going against what used to be a journalist‘s ethic for neutrality. 
I live in Germany, moved here from the US in ‚99. I was very impressed with the Tageschau anchors. They were focused on the events not the implications. Yes, they were dry and, for some, boring; but you got the NEWS not opinions. More and more, though, I feel that changing. More and more journalists think they are talk-show hosts, entitled to share their personal views with the audience. That is not what I expect from journalists. I expect well-researched facts and analysis NOT opinions. 
I now watch mostly just Tageschau and maybe a news hour from the US to keep informed. Anything more than that is pointless. It is enough to read the headlines (all you are allowed to read unless you subscribe online) to have a rough idea that … nothing has changed much since yesterday. And, even IF something major happens, there is no escaping it; it will be covered ad naseum everywhere anyway. 
I used to think my changing attitude was bad because I would be less informed. I am in total agreement with you: it is not information; it is just noise.
Thank you for being a sane voice. 🙏

author: @Amelia_PC
text:
Yes, agreed 100%, even in a very fragile situation.

Before this year, I completely avoided the news. I focused on work, caring for ill family members, and my creative process. Then a certain orange guy began spreading lies and attacking a neighboring country. So I started following the news.

I've worked remotely my entire life and depend entirely on foreign contracts. When this person threatened SWIFT wire transfers—essentially any dollar transaction—fear set in. Then came claims about using military force against any country with impunity. Venezuela came under attack over oil, justified by nonsensical narco-terrorism excuses—a sunken little boat allegedly carrying ALL cartel drugs bound for the US. A string of baseless accusations followed, and no country intervened.

This made me realize: if someone can target another country's water resources and still face no consequences, what's to stop them? I began imagining total isolation from international banking (which includes PayPal and Wise) and potential military confrontation over our water and rare metals. I panicked.

But then something clicked. 

I remembered I've always been a "third-world survivalist" who overcomes obstacles. I remembered that cryptocurrency exists without SWIFT dependency. I realized military confrontation could devastate the entire American continent, making economic isolation the more likely conflict. Most importantly, I remembered that every terrible problem has a solution—the only thing we can't fight is DEATH itself.

I calmed down and stopped reading the news. Honestly, I was exhausted from seeing that angry orange face everywhere. Enough.

(27:16 I'll never forget COVID. My healthy 60-year-old father died from the disease. When I got vaccinated, my body had severe reactions affecting multiple organs. This wasn't psychological—my non-verbal, level 3 autistic brother experienced identical symptoms after vaccination, despite having no understanding of COVID, vaccines, or what was happening to him. Our blood tests showed significant changes before and after vaccination. Most people are lucky not to be affected by COVID.)

author: @lak1294
text:
For me, the really big question is: when you feel your worthiness and whole-heartedness, what do you do when all you see and feel around you is distancing, disconnection, lack of empathy, and cowardice? Especially within your own family? What if you have good friends but not enough of them? What if you struggle to have a successful relationship?

I've done years of personal study and self-reflection to understand these things, and my own part in it. But I see more divisiveness, self-absorption, maladaption, and unwillingness of others to engage meaningfully. This is an epidemic in our modern culture. Things are trending towards more isolation and intolerance, not less. So it's bloody difficult to find connection now.

author: @aluumina
text:
My notes 

Connection vs disconnection
- shame and fear 
- Shame - the fear of disconnection (if ppl see this about me they won't want to connect with me)
- 5:30 extricating vulnerability = how u defeat shame 
- sense of worthiness 
- folks: 2 types. Sense of love and belonging vs those who don't.
- 7:23 - the one variable separating these two groups is the belief that they are worthy of love and belonging. That's it. You believe you are worthy.
- 8:48 what did these "whole hearted" people all have in common? 
- 8:50 courage* - they had the courage to to be imperfect. They had compassion* to be kind to themselves first, then to others. They had connection* as a result of authenticity (letting go of who you should be to embrace you you ARE.) 
- courage - tell the story of who you are with your whole heart
- 10:00 - they also had vulnerability* they believe what made them vulnerable made them beautiful. It's not easy or comfortable though, but there people talked about it being "necessary". So be who r u and stop controlling and predicting 
- 16:30 the issue: when we numb the bad stuff (ex: shame) we numb the good stuff too (ex: joy and happiness) 
- 19:13 let yourself be seen. To love with your whole heart even though there's no guarantee of a return (this is veryyyyyyyy hard). To practise gratitude and joy (to be able to feel this vulnerable means ur alive!). To believe that you are enough (in yourself, in your workplace, etc.)
- 



Here's my conclusion. She didn't say this outright so I'll try to put together the pieces myself. Being vulnerable is extremely important in being connected (with others and without ourselves). How? By defeating shame, which is this fear of disconnection (hide this because if ppl knew they wouldn't like me). How? The research shows if you want this to be "easy" (i.e. to do this being a 'whole hearted' person) then you need to believe you are worthy of love and belonging.

This is hard. But we can break it down a bit. These ppl had: 
- courage. To be imperfect.
- compassion - to be kind to themselves first, then to others
- connection - as a result of authenticity (letting go of who you should be to embrace you you ARE.) 

This is not easy and requires a lot of personal work, speaking from experience. But in a nutshell, this is you accepting and tolerating yourself (by having empathy for what you went through as a kid) and therefore also learning to tolerate others. And in the realm of compassion, learning this teaches you to accept yourself and like yourself, leading to a sense of yes, you are worthy of love. And this makes you unafraid of being who you really are - with all your imperfections included, leading to no or minimal shame, leading to being vulnerable (and this being easy). 

Hope this helps!

text:
Here are some of the highlights from the video that resonated with me a lot:

1. 3:26 - Connection is what gives meaning and purpose to our lives
2. 4:45 - Shame is the fear of disconnection. Is there something about me that if other people see it, I won’t be worthy of connection?
3. 5:15 - Shame is underpinned by this feeling of “I’m not good enough” or “I’m not _____ enough”
4. 5:30 - Excruciating vulnerability = For connection to happen we need to allow ourselves to be seen
5. 7:00 - People who have a sense of worthiness have a strong sense of love and belonging
6. 7:20 - People who have a strong sense of love and belonging *believe* they are worthy of love and belonging
7. 7:35 - The one thing that keeps us out of connection is the fear that we are not worthy of connection
8. 8:15 - People with a deep sense of worthiness are wholehearted people
9. 9:00 - Courage originally meant to tell the story of who you are with your whole heart. 
10. 9:10 - Wholehearted people have the courage to be imperfect, and have the compassion to be kind to themselves first and then to others.
11. 9:20 - We can’t practice compassion with other people if we can treat ourselves kindly. They had connection […] as a result of authenticity.
12. 9:30 - They were willing to let go of who they thought they should be in order to be who they were.
13. 9:50 - They fully embraced vulnerability. They believed that what made them vulnerable made them beautiful.
14. 10:15 - They didn’t talk about vulnerability being comfortable or excruciating. […] They talked about it being necessary.
15. 12:40 - Vulnerability is the core of shame, fear and our struggle for worthiness. It’s also the birthplace of joy, creativity, of belonging and love.
16. 14:40 - We numb vulnerability.
17. 15:50 - You cannot selectively numb emotion.
18. 16:20 - When you numb hard feelings, you numb joy, gratitude and happiness. 
19. 17:30 - Blame is a way to discharge pain and discomfort.
20. 19:10 - Let yourself be seen, deeply seen. Love with your whole heart even though there’s no guarantee.
21. 19:55 - Believe that we’re enough. “I am enough.”

author: @annamusicandart
text:
This talk is everything. Thank you, Brené, for bringing such depth and clarity to something that is so essential—and yet so counterintuitive—especially for those of us in the performing arts. As performers, we’re often taught to hide our vulnerability behind technique, perfection, or persona. Yet it’s vulnerability—the raw, unfiltered humanness—that truly moves audiences and creates art that heals, not just entertains. In my own journey as a performing artist and now as a transformational coach for artists, I’ve seen how deeply this message resonates—how many brilliant, successful performers feel isolated, anxious, or disconnected behind the curtain of their success. Vulnerability, when embraced safely and consciously, becomes not a weakness—but a superpower.
This talk continues to change lives. And it’s helping shift an entire industry toward more truth, more courage, and more soul-led expression. 🙏

He has the courageous panache to express his appreciation of these people to them verbally, giving them a perspective worth smiling about. When he meets the woman whose smile he most longs to behold, The tale goes amiss, but in the end the smile of his princess wins back his lost hope as he wins her heart, and they ride off into the sunset smiling side-by-side. Add your own laughter, tears, and multiple smiles by appreciating this film, too. Genius short film with feature length heart and soul. It will change you if you let it.

author: @rorytriscuit
text:
949 people need to be validated.

You are awesome. You are loved. You may think this is just a sappy video and that people need to just pull themselves up by their bootstraps and stop being so emotional. But that's not the case. It's time for you to feel what you feel. Are you truly happy? Recognize that you have become hardened because the world seems so cruel. Yes, the world is cruel. But someone out there loves you. Someone cares about your well-being. You have value. You feel lost and alone because you're scared to feel. You will deny my words with all your strength because you don't want to appear weak. Stop. Stop worrying about your image. Start worrying about your happiness. It is not on you to prove to the world that you are superior. It is on the world to accept you for your genuine self. You have a right to your emotions. You have a right to be your genuine self. And whether that be assholish or not (I, too, have my bitchy side), people WILL appreciate you for being super honest. Just be you. Yes, in certain roles we must all conform, but when it comes to matters of love and friendship... don't play a game. Just be real. You might be surprised just how happy you become when you find someone who gets you, accepts you, and supports you for being the person you currently are and the person you want to be. Find someone who inspires you to go down that path. You can find happiness. You can be a better person. You can experience the joys of true love (platonic or romantic). It's time for you to love yourself. You deserve it.

author: @Philscbx
text:
Now Seventy, probably wont be long, but I like how the older gent made a mark from the bench. 

Ive had unique visits similar, when a very special child of friend was taken by car accident- after the funeral, I walked out of church alone towards my car, and this special little 9 yr old girl performed the coolest whirl wind around me enough to russle the trees nearby. 

I could tell it was her, we spent such special times together when Id stop by to visit the family at small deep woods farm. 

I havent even gotten out of car yet, and she jumps on bicycle to greet me, and when she pulls up I notice both her tires are flat,  What the Hell,, come with me, and in the barn is airtank, and she cant believe how nice it is. Smiling at every crank of pedals... 

So I get request to weld up the cracked engine block on the tractor, And gather tools to remove items, and just about dark, she climbs up sitting on top of tractor, and cant wait to hold Flashlight to assist like any nurse during operation. 

Later, having diner, she'd climb up in my lap for a Fav'd book story and we both fall asleep after a long day. 
And a tough day by morning, rushing 55 miles to the airport to service airliner fleet of L-1011's for another round trip for 350 people back to Mpls Mn. 

Then I just get home and get a call shes just been killed running across the road to the little country store to save her dog.  
I was so devastated, and that was mid eighties. Nothing was ever the same again.  I couldnt go to that little farm again. 
I had to keep her memory alive just as I left that day. 
It changed them as well. 

But, one could make a unique short film - and hopefully duplicate the intense whirlwind that others never noticed. 
How it wrapped you with an energy that gently lifted upward. 
That would be her special style with added  effects of gathering leaves in the mix in gravel parking lot of the  church.  You stand there for a while, just to make sure no detail is missed. 
Cheers

author: @stormdrain23
text:
I’m not just quitting social media. I’m quitting my smart phone, because the problem goes beyond social media. I really think things started going south the moment we had ALL the information available to humanity in our pockets and that technology became widely available.

There is benefit - maybe even critical importance - in allowing a little bit of friction in our lives. There being an app for everything has short circuited our ability to allow for a bit of frustration and slow down - to enable us to disconnect. We’re so caught up in how “convenient” it is to have everything on our phones that we’ve learned helplessness. We’re don’t just embrace the convenience, we’re DEPENDENT on our phones for everything from spatial awareness, to concentration, to basic math. It’s a ball and chain - an anchor. I’m moving on.

Our phones fill our lives with so much noise - literal and figurative - that we can’t think anymore. We can’t tolerate boredom or silence. If it’s not social media, it’s videos, or music, or literally just mindlessly scrolling a web browser. It numbs the pleasure centers of our brains and makes it impossible to even enjoy life in the few moments when we are disconnected.

The AI nonsense started to really turn me off of technology. But one day I looked around while I was out with my kids and every parent was locked in on their phones… myself included. It was bone chilling.

author: @AbroadinJapan
text:
Excellent video man and great to see Jack Conte still going strong.
It's been disconcerting witnessing this both as a guy who's been consuming content on social media since 2005 and someone who's been producing videos 13 years on Youtube. Facebook and Twitter are completely and utterly unusable, while Instagram has turned from a genuinely good, social photo sharing app into a wannabe Tiktok. 
While Youtube is the best of the bunch, it's in danger of going down the same path. Shorts are being rammed everywhere. Meanwhile, it feels like subscribing to a channel has become redundant, as it's no guarantee you'll see that content on your feed.
On a creator level, where once all your videos were shared with your viewers organically, these days you've got to battle for the privilege. You need to ensure your video has a high click-through rate immediately. As a Youtuber this means the incentive to take risks on niche projects or ideas has disappeared, as you know a low click through rate will bury your video on the platform. Risk taking and originality is growing ever harder to justify with each passing year.
All this has certainly sapped the magic out of Youtube these last 3 years for me. As for the other socials, using them far less has made me a lot happier. It's better time spend walking, watching films or reading!

author: @flower.sunshinemama
text:
I’m glad I’m not the only one who stepped away from social media. Honestly, I’ve been so much happier since I left. The only exception I’ve kept is YouTube; I don’t really consider it the same as other platforms. At least with YouTube, you actually have some control: you can subscribe to what you like, block what you don’t, and the content leans more toward your actual interests. Plus, the longer videos help retrain your brain to move away from the short-attention-span stuff.

Most of Gen Z’s struggles trace back to social media. I used to think of myself as introverted, antisocial, and painfully awkward—like I could only interact with people online. But since I’ve been off those apps, it’s changed everything. I don’t obsess about my looks or body image anymore. When I go out, I see actual people—not filtered versions of them—and it feels real. I can interact with others more naturally now. I’m not suddenly an extrovert, but I do feel more “normal.” I don't think we're all as introverted as we think.

I’ve stopped focusing on what I don’t have or comparing myself to fake lives online. Instead, I’m working on myself, and the people around me have noticed a night-and-day difference. It’s not easy at first, but leaving social media for me was the key to actually living.

author: @lukebendallmusic
text:
My personal problem is the difficulty of being both a creator and a consumer. I'm constantly trying to reach views, audiences and more subs in the hope that something works out, but at the same time, I don't do trendy or viral style content that I see on tiktok and youtube. We are literally being fed videos that say "use this sound and you'll become viral", "make a video that's so short, you will get lots of views because of it" or literally using the word viral to make something viral. 
As a consumer, it's really boring me to see the lack of original content being pushed on these platforms. As a creator, it's completely messed with how I view my own content. I'm constantly checking views, likes, comments on all the platforms in the hope something just works. What that's ended up doing is creating a bad mentality that focuses on numbers and pleasing the algorithm instead of just being proud of what I made in the first place without seeking viral attention. 

I've ended up deleting all of my apps of social media, with the intention of just uploading videos and content when I want, but not giving myself the ability to see stats. The current system causes so many problems, including anxiety, OCD and depression that wasn't there before. I've felt the worst I've been in years after realising that what I'm doing and being fed is a cocktail of digital cringe and viral success overnight. 
Hopefully, I can get that time back that I usually waste on social media to do something more productive. Making more music, making tracks that don't even need to be released (but just for fun), coming up with fun video idea's that I want to do without thinking of its success, or even putting more time towards trying to learn Japanese over the next few years.

Social media is no longer the cool and amazing thing it once was. Our friends don't realise that they don't care about what we post, as they doom scroll until they see something that might be funny to share, send it, then continue. Growing up with it didn't seem as bad, but the last couple of years has just had a dramatic decline on my mental heath, which I have already worked on so hard to keep in a good place.

Here's hoping that things change, but seeing these companies in an infinite loop of trying to get more cash grabs and data out of us makes me wonder if they have realised how bad they've gotten.

Excuses I make to myself when I procrastinate:

"I'll have time later" (when I won't)
"I'm still brainstorming" (When I've spent 75% of the project "brainstorming")
"I'll start soon"
"After I finish this game"

"I'll just have a short break"
"It's not that much work"
"If it gets bad I'll request a due date extension" 
"I've earned a mental health break, I'll just do it in an hour" (When I've done nothing to earn a mental health break and I certainly know I won't do it in an hour)
"I'm done with my homework" (When I myself know I'm not)
I've even gone as far as to purposefully disconnect my internet or "lose" my school bag just to have an excuse to not do work. 

Why I lie to myself when I know it's a lie is beyond me, it's an unhealthy and stupid habit of mine but I can't get rid of it.

text:
I agree with the claim about using those 8 steps will help you be successful in your up coming future. The casual reasoning behind each one of those steps is strong because one thing caused the other to happen. For example, when he explains the part about "when you do it for love you get the money anyway." This shows casual reasoning because if you love what you do the money part just falls into place because of all your hard work you put into it. (Logos Casual Reasoning) 
       The points the man made in this Ted Talk were so strong that I am inspired. I want to love and have passion for my job when I get old. As I grow older I will keep these 8 points in my mind. I will learn to not have self doubt and be passionate about what I do with my life. (Intrinsic Ethos)
       As I grew up I learned that completely hating you job and what you do for a living is not the way to go. My father for example when he first started working in construction he loved it. He loved learning how to work new machines, digging holes and getting around in tight spaces. Now that he older and knows how to do every single one of those things to perfection he hates it. He wakes up at 5 in the morning to go to a job he doesn't even enjoy going to. This is why it is so important for me to be successful in life. I want to love what I do wit my life I want to enjoy every little bit of it and this is why I will be using these 8 steps of success for the rest  of my life. (Pathos)

text: One thing I agree with is that you can never see how the dots of life will connect looking forward and looking back at my age, it surprises me how I am here today as a student and especially a freshman. Looking can back I see how important it is to love what you do. When you find something that makes you feel good when you're doing it, and you want to do it more and more, then that is what you should spend your time doing. That is how you don't get burned out in life and get discouraged. Find what you love and stick to it no matter the challenges that come up. Life is short looking back and when you're looking forward it seems like it will take too long to make the things you want to happen. Everyday will pass anyway. so you may as well figure out what makes you happy early. it is also funny how you can start out doing one thing that will lead you to doing another thing. You never know how the dots are going to connect, so just keep seeking and when you find that love, stick to it.

author: @仙狐さん大好き
text:
学生にした2時間のプレゼンをここでは3分間で話します。
TEDに来る飛行機でのこと。
7年前でした。
隣は高校生、10代だったかな。
彼女は貧乏な家の生まれで「何かで成功したい」と打ち明けてきました。
そして、素朴な質問をしました。
「どうしたら成功できるの？」
でも僕は答えられず、申し訳なくなりました。
その直後にTEDに来て、ひらめいたのです！
見渡す限り、成功者ばかりじゃないか！
ここで成功の秘密を聴き、それを子供たちに伝えよう。
そして7年間で500人にインタビューをした今お答えします！成功の秘密は何か？
何がTEDメンバーを突き動かすのか？
1つ目は、熱意。
フリーマン・トーマス「熱意こそ私の原動力」
TEDメンバーは好きだからやっている。お金が目的ではない。
キャラル・コレット「人を雇っても、今やっていることをやりたい」
さらに面白いのは熱意に従えば、お金は後からついてくる。
働く！ルパート・マードック「全力でやろう。簡単なことなどないが、やっていてとても楽しい」
ルパートは「楽しい」だって？！その通り！
TEDメンバーは楽しみながらよく働く。
彼らは仕事中毒ではなく、仕事オタクです。
特技！アレックス・ガーデン「成功するために、特技を持とう」
近道はない。単に　練習！練習！練習！
一点集中。ノーマン・ジュイソン曰く「すべきことは、1つのことに集中することだ」
押す！デイビット・ガロ「自分を後押ししよう。物理的にも　精神的にも　押す！押す！押す！」
恥や自信の無さは、押しだそう！
ゴールディ・ホーン「自信がなかった頃　私はこう言っていました」
「不器用だし　頭も悪いからきっと成功なんてしないわ」
自分で押し続けるのは大変だから人々は母親を発明しました。
フランク・ゲリーはこう答えました！
「うちの母親がやらせた」
役に立とう！シャーマン・ヌーランド「医者として役に立てたのは光栄でした」
たくさんの子供が億万長者になりたいと言ってきます。
そこでまず、答えるのは
「自分の役にたつというのは無理だから他人の役にたつ何かを与えましょう。
それが唯一　大金持ちになれる方法です」
アイデア！TEDメンバーのビル・ゲイツ曰く
「世界初のパソコンソフト会社を創りたいと思った」
それは良いアイデアだと僕も思うよ。
発想力をつけるのに近道などありません。
基本をやり続けるのみです。
それらはこのようなことです。
貫徹する！ジョー・クラウス曰く「貫徹することで私たちは成功できた」
失敗してもやり通す。「向かい風」の中でも貫徹する！
「向かい風」とは　批判　無視　馬鹿　プレッシャー！
もっともな答えは　シンプル！
4000ドル払ってTEDに来よう！
それが無理だとしたら　これら8つを続けよう！
これら8つが成功の秘密です。
インタビューを受けてくれたTEDメンバー　有難う！

author: @micoyap100
text:
I’ve been looking for something like this for a long time.

This is exactly what I do in school and I’ve always wonder if other people have done it. It makes studying extremely fun and you retain the material longer the stronger the story is. Emphasize on emotion (fun, sad, anger) as your brain will retain that information for a long time.

For me, what I’ve done is I create fictional characters and tie them to a story and relate it to a material.
For my personal example: I would link restriction enzyme (enzyme that cuts DNA) to a story such as one of my characters slicing a DNA with a sword. Now whenever someone mentions restriction enzyme I think of that.

These fictional characters are precious to me and I absolutely love them. They came from a variety of genre that I enjoy. Now link a material to a story where that precious character dies and see if that material doesn’t engrave on your mind. I sound like a weirdo but it works for me.

author: @perikaveera4438
text:
I am a physician, M.D. in Mississippi and would like to share my experience here. I've been in the United States for 25 years but I was born and raised in Bombay, India which I visit every couple of years. Now, India is a multilingual country and Bombay is the most cosmopolitan Indian city where several languages are spoken. Ever since I can remember, I was exposed to 6 languages including English (education though, was exclusively in English with French and the vernacular lingo being an optional subject, and that too starting only in the 5th grade). Besides English (&French) at school and with friends, by the age of 3 or 4 I could also speak Hindi (+read/write), Marathi (+read/write), Telugu and Gujarati fluently. And each of these languages in 2 or 3 different regional dialects. As for Chinese, we had a small ethnic Chinese minority in Bombay who spoke Mandarin Chinese at home (only speak, not read/write) and English and 2 or 3 local Indian languages. I've been away from India for 25 years and living in South Mississippi, hardly ever get to speak the Indian languages and YET, I have not lost my fluency in these. My American friends, co-workers and office staff are amazed at this ability of mine and say "Doc, you're a doctor, you're smart and that's why". If I was indeed so smart I would not have been struggling with Spanish considering that 20% of my patients are Latino and I still sometimes need my office translator to whom I pay $27000 a year!
Bottom line is that as a child, toddler, your brain's capacity to learn things is infinite but as an adult, it's very limited. In Medical School, by the time you've passed your Ist year and successive years, you've forgotten 70% of what you've learned during the previous year. Left me saying to myself, if I could learn and remember 6 languages by the time I was 4 or 5, why not my medical subjects??
Jackson, Mississippi.﻿

author: @MaoDev
text:
Here I have the trick to remember any number!


You have to know how to store the numbers into words and then use the trick in the video  (to imagine the words as an animation).
Anyway, to store numbers into words you have to assign the digits to the letters that look the most similar to them. For example: 1893 = "IBgE" which is already a lot easier to remember. Now you can  also convert those letters to an actual word or a sentence,  therefore IBgE = "I Beat Grandma's Ex" or "I Beg Give monEEEEEEy!" which is even easier to remember now if you store the numbers into words and sentences that are ridiculous. The actual challenge is to come up with those  words and sentences actually fast. If you can do that then you are most likely to rarely forget a number. The last step is to imagine the words as an animation and there you go. You found immortality, CONGRATULATIONS!

The more connections in makes with different neurons, the more connections that have to be broken for you to forget. You can keep trying to strengthen the connection between the same two neurons but lots of connections will be better than fewer connections that are a bit stronger.

author: @hoanghuy385
text:
**THE FIRST 20 HOURS - HOW TO LEARN ANYTHING**

1. Deconstruct the skill:
    - decide exactly what you want to be able to do when you're done, and then look into the skill and break it down into smaller pieces.
2. Learn enough to self correct:
    - learn just enough that you can actually practice and self correct or self edit as you practice.
3. Remove barriers to practice:
    - remove the distractions that are keeping you from practicing.
4. Practice for at least 20 hours:
    - by pre-committing to practicing whatever it is that you want to do for at least 20 hours, you will be able to overcome initial frustration barrier and stick with the practice long enough to actually reap the rewards.
5. The major barrier's not intellectual, it's emotional.

author: @QuickTalks
text:
Summary: Just 20 hours is enough to become “reasonably good” at any skill. 

1. Deconstruct the skill - Break the skill down into its most basic parts. Which parts are necessary for hitting the goal you have? (i.e. if your goal is to sing a song in Korean, you can primarily focus on pronunciation, not learning a bunch of vocabulary)
2. Learn enough to self correct - Learn enough to realize when you're making mistakes.
3. Remove barriers to practice - Turn off your phone, unplug the TV. Put your guitar, piano, language book in the middle of your room, not behind your stack of dirty laundry.
4. Practice for at least 20 hours - Commit to 20 hours from the start. You're going to be frustrated at times, so committing beforehand will help you push through the frustration.

author: @David-bz7pi
text:
I think this is a good video, and I appreciated it being put up.  Some of the comments really make me wonder how pessimistic people can really be.

One of the largest problems for people trying something new is willpower.  It may be based off "feeling stupid", but it's more likely based off of being lazy when the immediate gains aren't met.  When learning something new, there's a stumbling period, and yes that feels really bad.  The purpose of this video, the purpose of the 20 hours is not to gain *mastery* into something, but to at least gain some level of skill outside of absolute stumbling beginner.  If you're learning a language, 20 hours will not make you conversational, but you will be to a point where you feel confident where you're going.

Lots of other programs out there try a similar approach to this 20-hours thing he puts together.  P90X, T25 are two examples.  In P90X, you have 90 days of workouts lined up for you to do.  You simply "press play" and go.  With T25, it's 60 days.  My point in this is that if you can commit to a certain period of time, and really concentrate on making it that time without thinking about how good or bad you are at something, you'll be surprised where you end up at after 20 hours.  This is all about getting over the "willpower" hump.

One thing I think is important that he said...and that's the whole "45m per day" thing.  Consistency is *really* important.  45 minutes a day is better than hours on one day of the week.  This is especially true while learning something.  An old coworker really put this well.  "Small amounts of time, every day, lead to really great results".

text: I've been using a variation of this technique for 30 years to teach newbies programming. I call it the building block approach. Essentially teach a small aspect of the programming language at a time, get the "student" to use it over and over while being productive for their team. When each building block is mastered move to the next one. In a relative short period of time the student becomes an independent and productive programmer. So, instead of a steep learning curve, there are many short learning curves. Each building block aligns with Kaufman's 20 hours of practice. Thank you Josh!

author: @luisfernandogarcia6974
text:
1 - decida exatamente o que você quer ser capaz de fazer quando você abacar, e então olhe para a habilidade e divida-a em pequenos pedaços. A maior parte das habilidades que queremos aprender, na verdade são grandes pacotes de habilidades que requerem diferentes coisas. Quanto mais dividirmos essa habilidade,  mais somos capazes de decidir quais são as partes da habilidade que irão realmente nos ajudar a conseguirmos o que queremos. E dessa forma podemos praticar primeiro as coisas mais importantes, e dessa forma seremos capazes de melhorar a nossa performance no menor tempo possível.
2 - a segunda é, aprender o suficiente para se auto-corrigir. Então, devemos pegar de três a cinco recursos sobre o que estamos tentando aprender. Pode ser livros, DVDs, cursos, qualquer coisa. Não devemos usar isso como forma de adiar a prática. A prática deve começar imediatamente, e o que queremos é aprender o suficiente para sermos capazes de nos auto-corrigirmos ou auto-editarmos enquanto praticamos. Então o aprendizado se torna uma forma de melhorar e notar quando estamos cometendo um erro, e dessa forma podemos fazer algo diferente.
3 - remova as barreiras para praticar. Distrações, televisão, internet, todas essas coisas que ficam no caminho entre nós e a cadeira para começarmos a estudar e trabalhar. Dessa forma, quanto mais nos tornamos capazes de usar um pouco da nossa força de vontade para remover as distrações que estão impedindo de praticar mais somos capazes de sentar e praticarmos. 
4 - praticar por pelo menos 20 horas.

author: @MilkySandwich
text:
10,000 hours to master a new skill  - watch it ! 
20 hours to be reasonably good at something – IF you apply 4 steps : 
1. Deconstruct skill – start with the most important parts first
2. Learn enough to self-correct 
3. Remove practice barriers/distractions – TV, internet 
4. Practice minimum 20 hours – the barrier here is the frustration that comes from the lack of knowledge : we suck and we know it. Doing 20h might seem short, but intense focus is actually hard to maintain, because of emotional junk. 
The major barrier to skill acquisition is not intellectual – it’s emotional.

author: @ronaldojr3935
text:
Minhas anotações:

1.Decompor a habilidade: Decida exatamente o que você quer ser capaz de fazer quando você acabar, e então olhe para a habilidade e divida-a em pequenos pedaços. A maioria das coisas que você pensar como uma habilidade são na verdade grandes pacotes de habilidades que requerem diferentes coisas. Quanto mais você dividir essa habilidade, mais você é capaz de decidir, quais são as partes da habilidade que irão realmente te ajudar a conseguir o que eu quero. E então você pode praticar essas coisas. E se você praticar a coisa mais importante primeiro, você vai ser capaz de melhorar a sua performance no menor tempo possível.

2.Aprender o suficiente para se auto-corrigir. Então, pegue três a cinco recursos sobre oque você está tentando aprender. Pode ser Livro, podem ser DVDS, podem ser Cursos, pode ser qualquer coisa. Mas não use isso como uma forma de adiar a prática. O que você quer é aprender o suficiente que você pode praticar e se auto corrigir ou auto-editar enquanto você pratica. Então o aprendizado se torna uma forma de melhorar e notar quando você está cometendo um erro e então fazer algo um pouco diferente.

3.Remover as barreiras para praticar. Distrações, televisão, internet. Todas essas coisas que ficam no caminho entre você sentar e começar a trabalhar. E quanto mais você se torna capaz de usar um pouco de sua força de vontade para remover as distrações que estão impedindo de praticar, mais você é capaz de sentar e praticar.

4.Praticar por pelo menos 20 horas. A maioria das habilidades tem oque eu chamo de barreira de frustração. Se sentir estupido é uma barreira que nos impede de sentar e fazer o trabalho. Então por se comprometer a praticar oque for que você quer fazer por pelo menos 20 horas, você vai ser capaz de superar aquela barreira de frustração inicial e se manter na prática tempo suficiente para colher a recompensa.

author: @Bitter_Biscuit
text:
Notes and summary for myself

The seven deadly sins of Speaking

    1. Gossip: Speaking negatively about someone who is not present. People will not trust you because a while later, you will gossip about them.
    2. Judging: It is hard to listen to someone who consistently judge you during a conversation.
    3. Negativity: Having a negative viewpoint on things. 
    4. Complaining: which is mere viral misery. Could be on anything, politics, sports, or the weather.
    5. Excuses: Not taking responsibility for our actions and being a blame-thrower
    6. Exaggeration: Drawing an imaginary image and inflating stuff excessively. It can get to the point of outright **lying**.
    7. Dogmatism: stating your opinions as if they are facts without consideration of an evidence to support your claims. In other words, Bombarding people with biased opinions on a certain topic.


- Foundation of powerful speech (HAIL)

    1. Honesty: Being clear and straight. Not using deception and lies. But using brutal and unnecessary honesty could hurt people. "Honesty tempered with Love".
    2. Authenticity: Being yourself and not imitating a non-genuine persona. "Standing in your own truth".
    3. Integrity: Be your word. Do what you say. Be trustworthy, and take responsibility.
    4. Love: Wishing people well. No judgement.


- Toolbox of Speech (Voice)

    1. Register: Talk from your chest, not the nose or throat. "We vote for the politicians with lower voices". People associate depth with power and authority.
    2. Timbre: The way the voice feels. "Rich, Smooth, Warm, like hot chocolate." It is a skill that can be trained.
    3. Prosody: Talking with enthusiasm, having a rhythmic voice, and not being monotonic like a robot. Avoid repetitive prosody as if every statement was a question.
    4. Pace: Talk normally and slow right down to... *Emphasize*. Talking fast or slow at the right time is key in conveying your point.
    5. Silence: A powerful tool to bring attention. Should not be filled with filler words such as UH's and UM's.
    6. Pitch: To deliver an idea or ask a question and being understood. (The caps-lock of speech)
    7. Volume: The quieter the better in bringing attention. But don't be too quiet all the time and don't be a broadcaster too. Pay attention to your loudness.


- Warm up the toolbox of voice

    1. Arms up, take a deep breath and sigh.
    2. Lips: (BA BA BA)
    3. Lips: Horse sound
    4. Tongue: Exaggerated (LA LA LA)
    5. Tongue: Roll an R (RRRRR)
    6. The siren (WEEEE [High] yoooo [Low])

Speaking is one part of the puzzle because having a good conversation also depends on being a good listener.

Edit: Reconstructed the phrasing of the point of dogmatism.
Thank you for all the beautiful replies.Happy to make your day a bit easier :)

author: @NguyenThu-ls1lb
text: The human voice: It's the instrument we all play. It's the most powerful sound in the world, probably. It's the only one that can start a war or say "I love you." And yet many people have the experience that when they speak, people don't listen to them. And why is that? How can we speak powerfully to make change in the world? What I'd like to suggest, there are a number of habits that we need to move away from. I've assembled for your pleasure here seven deadly sins of speaking. I'm not pretending this is an exhaustive list, but these seven, I think, are pretty large habits that we can all fall into. First, gossip. Speaking ill of somebody who's not present. Not a nice habit, and we know perfectly well the person gossiping, five minutes later, will be gossiping about us. Second, judging. We know people who are like this in conversation, and it's very hard to listen to somebody if you know that you're being judged and found wanting at the same time. Third, negativity. You can fall into this. My mother, in the last years of her life, became very negative, and it's hard to listen. I remember one day, I said to her, "It's October 1 today," and she said, "I know, isn't it dreadful?" (Laughter) It's hard to listen when somebody's that negative. (Laughter) And another form of negativity, complaining. Well, this is the national art of the U.K. It's our national sport. We complain about the weather, sport, about politics, about everything, but actually, complaining is viral misery. It's not spreading sunshine and lightness in the world. Excuses. We've all met this guy. Maybe we've all been this guy. Some people have a blamethrower. They just pass it on to everybody else and don't take responsibility for their actions, and again, hard to listen to somebody who is being like that. Penultimate, the sixth of the seven, embroidery, exaggeration. It demeans our language, actually, sometimes. For example, if I see something that really is awesome, what do I call it? (Laughter) And then, of course, this exaggeration becomes lying, and we don't want to listen to people we know are lying to us. And finally, dogmatism. The confusion of facts with opinions. When those two things get conflated, you're listening into the wind. You know, somebody is bombarding you with their opinions as if they were true. It's difficult to listen to that. So here they are, seven deadly sins of speaking. These are things I think we need to avoid. But is there a positive way to think about this? Yes, there is. I'd like to suggest that there are four really powerful cornerstones, foundations, that we can stand on if we want our speech to be powerful and to make change in the world. Fortunately, these things spell a word. The word is "hail," and it has a great definition as well. I'm not talking about the stuff that falls from the sky and hits you on the head. I'm talking about this definition, to greet or acclaim enthusiastically, which is how I think our words will be received if we stand on these four things. So what do they stand for? See if you can guess. The H, honesty, of course, being true in what you say, being straight and clear. The A is authenticity, just being yourself. A friend of mine described it as standing in your own truth, which I think is a lovely way to put it. The I is integrity, being your word, actually doing what you say, and being somebody people can trust. And the L is love. I don't mean romantic love, but I do mean wishing people well, for two reasons. First of all, I think absolute honesty may not be what we want. I mean, my goodness, you look ugly this morning. Perhaps that's not necessary. Tempered with love, of course, honesty is a great thing. But also, if you're really wishing somebody well, it's very hard to judge them at the same time. I'm not even sure you can do those two things simultaneously. So hail. Also, now that's what you say, and it's like the old song, it is what you say, it's also the way that you say it. You have an amazing toolbox. This instrument is incredible, and yet this is a toolbox that very few people have ever opened. I'd like to have a little rummage in there with you now and just pull a few tools out that you might like to take away and play with, which will increase the power of your speaking. Register, for example. Now, falsetto register may not be very useful most of the time, but there's a register in between. I'm not going to get very technical about this for any of you who are voice coaches. You can locate your voice, however. So if I talk up here in my nose, you can hear the difference. If I go down here in my throat, which is where most of us speak from most of the time. But if you want weight, you need to go down here to the chest. You hear the difference? We vote for politicians with lower voices, it's true, because we associate depth with power and with authority. That's register. Then we have timbre. It's the way your voice feels. Again, the research shows that we prefer voices which are rich, smooth, warm, like hot chocolate. Well if that's not you, that's not the end of the world, because you can train. Go and get a voice coach. And there are amazing things you can do with breathing, with posture, and with exercises to improve the timbre of your voice. Then prosody. I love prosody. This is the sing-song, the meta-language that we use in order to impart meaning. It's root one for meaning in conversation. People who speak all on one note are really quite hard to listen to if they don't have any prosody at all. That's where the word "monotonic" comes from, or monotonous, monotone. Also, we have repetitive prosody now coming in, where every sentence ends as if it were a question when it's actually not a question, it's a statement? (Laughter) And if you repeat that one, it's actually restricting your ability to communicate through prosody, which I think is a shame, so let's try and break that habit. Pace. I can get very excited by saying something really quickly, or I can slow right down to emphasize, and at the end of that, of course, is our old friend silence. There's nothing wrong with a bit of silence in a talk, is there? We don't have to fill it with ums and ahs. It can be very powerful. Of course, pitch often goes along with pace to indicate arousal, but you can do it just with pitch. Where did you leave my keys? (Higher pitch) Where did you leave my keys? So, slightly different meaning in those two deliveries. And finally, volume. (Loud) I can get really excited by using volume. Sorry about that, if I startled anybody. Or, I can have you really pay attention by getting very quiet. Some people broadcast the whole time. Try not to do that. That's called sodcasting, (Laughter) Imposing your sound on people around you carelessly and inconsiderately. Not nice. Of course, where this all comes into play most of all is when you've got something really important to do. It might be standing on a stage like this and giving a talk to people. It might be proposing marriage, asking for a raise, a wedding speech. Whatever it is, if it's really important, you owe it to yourself to look at this toolbox and the engine that it's going to work on, and no engine works well without being warmed up. Warm up your voice. Actually, let me show you how to do that. Would you all like to stand up for a moment? I'm going to show you the six vocal warm-up exercises that I do before every talk I ever do. Any time you're going to talk to anybody important, do these. First, arms up, deep breath in, and sigh out, ahhhhh, like that. One more time. Ahhhh, very good. Now we're going to warm up our lips, and we're going to go Ba, Ba, Ba, Ba, Ba, Ba, Ba, Ba. Very good. And now, brrrrrrrrrr, just like when you were a kid. Brrrr. Now your lips should be coming alive. We're going to do the tongue next with exaggerated la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la, la. Beautiful. You're getting really good at this. And then, roll an R. Rrrrrrr. That's like champagne for the tongue. Finally, and if I can only do one, the pros call this the siren. It's really good. It starts with "we" and goes to "aw." The "we" is high, the "aw" is low. So you go, weeeaawww, weeeaawww. Fantastic. Give yourselves a round of applause. Take a seat, thank you. (Applause) Next time you speak, do those in advance. Now let me just put this in context to close. This is a serious point here. This is where we are now, right? We speak not very well to people who simply aren't listening in an environment that's all about noise and bad acoustics. I have talked about that on this stage in different phases. What would the world be like if we were speaking powerfully to people who were listening consciously in environments which were actually fit for purpose? Or to make that a bit larger, what would the world be like if we were creating sound consciously and consuming sound consciously and designing all our environments consciously for sound? That would be a world that does sound beautiful, and one where understanding would be the norm, and that is an idea worth spreading. Thank you. (Applause)

author: @NothingMaster
text: Excellent talk!  It shared many useful and practical techniques that are bound to help anyone.  The content of the message and the quality of the vocal delivery are exceedingly important, but they are not the only mechanisms by which one could entice people to listen.    I've found that there is a hidden amplifying magnet in that tool box that could exact a considerable impact on how willing people would be to listen to what you have to say---especially, when addressing smaller audiences---and that is 'eye contact'.   In an increasingly fast-paced and impatient world, it has become a serious challenge to grab and maintain people's attention long enough to communicate an idea.  The short attention span could be greatly remedied using effective eye contact strategies.  For example, I have tried to deliver the same talk to the same audience with and without effective eye contact and the difference between the two strategies has been quite dramatic.  When you don't establish effective eye contact with your audience, you quickly lose them to the bouts of distraction and impatience.

Really, everything mentioned is an excellent practice, but it's only useful when speaking with someone who practices the same principles.

7 sins of speaking:
gossip
judging
negativity
complaining
excuses, not taking responsibility
exaggeration, that can become lying
dogmatism, confusion of facts with opinions

H - honesty, be clear and straight
A - authenticity, be yourself
I - integrity, be your word, trustworthy
L - love, wish people well

Humans prefer voices, that are low(coming from chest), rich, warm, smooth. YOU can train to get there (coach, posture, breathing, exercises).
Change tones, to communicate meanings. Dont use wrong tonality and make it reflect what you are trying to communicate.

Silence
Pitch - how high
Volume - from  loud to quiet

lips coming alive "brrrr" like kids
tongue exaggerated "la, la, la, la"

author: @samarpiene
text:
Die Gewohnheiten, die wir ablegen können, wenn wir wollen, dass uns zugehört wird (0:50):
1. Klatsch und Tratsch
2. Urteilen
3. Negativität
4. Beschwerden
5. Entschuldigungen/Ausflüchte
6. Übertreibungen/Lügen
7. Dogmatismen, Verwechseln von Tatsachen und Meinungen

Wie statt dessen (HAIL)(3:20):
- Ehrlichkeit (sei korrekt, klar und deutlich - verbunden mit Liebe)
- Authentizität (sei du selbst)
- Integrität (handle wie du sprichst, sei vertrauenswürdig)
- Liebe (wünsche den Anderen Gutes)

Werkzeuge (4:38):
Stimmlage -  Sprich mit der Brust - Stimme, um dem Gesagten mehr Gewicht zu verleihen
Klangfarbe - reich, sanft, warm (kann man trainieren)
Satzrhythmus/Klangfülle - melodischer Singsang versus Monotonie/Eintönigkeit
Tempo - Unterstreichen des Gesagten durch Schnelligkeit oder Verlangsamung oder Schweigen/Stille
Tonhöhe - je nach Tonhöhe werden andere Emotionen transportiert 
Lautstärke - begeistert oder aufgeregt: hohes Volume, Aufmerksamkeit steigernd: leises Volume 

Ab 7:45 Aufwärm - Übungen für die Stimme

Bin sehr begeistert von dieser kurzen und würzigen Anleitung! Vielen Dank, Julian Treasure (was für ein Schatz!) und TED !
Allen Vorbeikommenden einen schönen Tag!

author: @TCMapotherIV
text: My experience with FSD Beta in a 2020 Model 3 Performance is that it's still not perfect but it's good enough to do about 80% of my driving. I still have to pay attention and take over sometimes but most of the issues are just annoying rather than dangerous. Some would be dangerous if I completely stopped paying attention. It's not good on undivided highways. In that situation, tends to think that a new lane of traffic is opening up every time a turn lane appears so it still changes into it even though I'm trying to continue straight. Until a couple of months ago it took a lot of unnecessary turns. That's rare now. Sometimes it's too cautious so it has trouble catching an exit in time or is slow to leave a stop so I have to hit the accelerator a little. It shows extreme promise and does seem to be on the path to be dramatically better than any other similar product available. The fact that it will work anywhere without premappng or other conditions for use (like the Mercedes system that's called Level 3 but can only drive on premapped highways up to 45 miles per hour) is huge. It should also be noted that an idiot tried to force his way in front of me going left as I went straight 2 months ago and caused some pretty bad front end damage. It took until a week ago for Tesla to take my car in for repair but my car continued to drive very well with Full Self Driving anyway. I happened to not be using FSD when I was hit. I was crossing a divided highway and I was already almost to the divider looking right to monitor the opposite side of traffic when he slammed into me. I would have noticed him in time to stop if I hadn't been looking right so had I been using FSD the accident would have likely been averted since it would have seen him making his moronic move in time to stop.

One honest question I have about full self-driving is, would it make a major difference or no difference at all to install sensors in the road in order for the car to read a sort of data algorithm in the road. 
For instance, perhaps a flat lying object with a barcode that forces the car to read active data from a network that you can install along the roadway that it reads as a sort of barcode, a sort of infrared beam that bounces back to the sort of allow the car to focus mostly on whats ahead, perhaps you could have a seperate network to allow for road crews, emergency crews, etc to send data to a network and your car can receive that data in real time, so that the car can predict those types of things and plan for it.
Would it be more effective to almost build road networks like that with the car in mind, kind of like we've done with sattelite internet networking, if we as humas just factor in that self driving cars WILL be a thing of the future, so we build our roads with these things in mind to make it almost foolproof so that we can focus more on how we solve the next level of anomalies, such as pedestrians crossing the road (crosswalks could not communicate with this system so that the car knows whats going on at an intersectiob) or an immediate accident ahead, or an object on or beside the roadway that might be potentially hazardous?

author: @herryhubert2706
text:
I am from Amsterdam, Netherlands, so some of my experiences may be a little different from most of you here. 
When I was in my teens, I was a punk and DIY was a very important part of it. This was in sharp contrast with the disco-kids, who were following fashion as much as they could. As a disco-kid you had to wear either Nikes or Adidas, Cool Cat, Kappa, etc etc. When I look back at this, it feels like if we were in some giant social research program. As if we were studied to see how easily we would adopt brands. How we would embrace a certain brand of shoes and next tell everybody about how much better these new shoes were. It turned out we were largely willing to be advertisement poles. We actually thought we were part of a higher species if we were able to buy the more expensive brands. I think this is where it all started.

If I look at how willing people are to buy a new smartphone by Apple or Samsung and spend an incredible amount of money on a device, while you have exactly the same functions in a device which is ⅓ of the price, but doesn't have the brandname on it. And when you point this out to them, they will defend their choices with a lot of religious sounding reasons, as if they are Jehowa Witnesses. Sometimes these more expensive phones have options that maybe handy, but it turns out they are hardly ever used. Or they want these highly annoying digi-watches, that are so convenient. I really hate it when I am together with someone, who's constantely checking his wrist. Back in the days, when you looked at your wrist, it meant you were getting bored, and were trying to use time to get away. Sometimes you don't even need such a watch. People are always staring at their screens, and I feel like shouting: "Hey, I am here!!! In real life! On the seat next to you!" But there's always something "important" they are afraid to miss.

Then on these phones there are apps. People hardly ever check what kind of personal information is stored by the companies that make those apps. I remember the conspiracy thinkers during Corona, who were afraid the government were to inject chips in them through the vaccination program. While those same conspiracists walked around with a smartphone in their pockets.
People accept cookies without giving it a second thought. Why do you think there's so much money involved in these tracking-companies. And why are there so many of these companies. And moreover, WTF is Legitimate Interest?

Last week my (dutch) bank send me a notice. They're going to stop "contact free payment" and replace it with "google pay". Why on earth do they think I would like some company like google, to serve my payments? Google already knows more than enough about me, and they have no right to peek into my spendings to personalize advertisement (which I think it the whole idea). But I am fairly sure that just about everybody will accept this because they either don't really think about the consequences or feel like they are powerless.

To cut a long story short: it is just us humans, addicted to consumerism and supposed luxury, who gave all the power to these companies.

Professors Martin Gilens (Princeton University) and Benjamin I. Page (Northwestern University) looked at more than 20 years worth of data to answer a simple question: Does the government represent the people?

What they found was extremely unsettling: The opinions of 90% of Americans have essentially no impact at all.
