author: @alexschott2092
text:
We've seen the two technology futures Mr. Bremmer has proposed featured prominently in sci-fi for decades. On the optimistic side, you have entries like _Star Trek_ where, despite the worst of our baser nature inflicting havoc on our species and planet, we were able to learn and grow alongside our technological advancements to forge a better society.

On the pessimistic side, you have series like _Blade Runner_ and _Cyberpunk 2077_ where corporations and the economies they create are the government in all but name. Ethics and basic means for survival become malleable, controlled commodities to sell to increasingly impoverished masses desperate for any escape from the dystopia they cannot escape. And they will insulate themselves with seemingly endless layers of physical, legal, and digital defenses to ensure nobody but them gains access to their kingdoms.

There's also other variations on this scale, like _Metal Gear Solid_ and _Metal Gear Rising_ with mankind's own nature and desire for control literally becoming digital overlords that try controlling the very chaos of their existence. It doesn't last forever, obviously, but the impact it leave on the world creates opportunities both good and ill (depending on how those wielding such power).

It'll be interesting to see what end of the spectrum the next few decades will place us on.

author: @AlexanderGrodskij
text:
Firstly, the prospect of unilateral American military domination seems increasingly unlikely. Just five months ago, the narrative suggested that Russia was on the losing side in the Ukraine conflict. However, the current situation is far less certain. The emergence of a military alliance comprising China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea could potentially reshape the global geopolitical landscape into two distinct military orders. This perspective differs from Ian Bremmer's viewpoint presented in his talk.

Turning to digital companies, it's crucial to recognize their integral role in society. These companies are comprised of citizens from various nations, with a significant majority being U.S. citizens. It's important to note that these entities, despite their global reach, remain subject to the laws of their home countries. Legal violations can result in individuals associated with these companies facing imprisonment. Consequently, the idea that digital companies could autonomously dominate the world is improbable. They will invariably adhere to and comply with the regulatory frameworks imposed upon them.

author: @Thecriticalthinker02
text:
Dr. Justin Mosley' lecture about the fear of public speaking was relatable. Firstly, he reiterated that we all have something unique to say that other people will learn from immensely. This realization gives us the righting power to see our experiences as valuable.

Mosley also emphasizes the need for us to turn the spotlight away from ourselves and to our audience in building some sense of purpose into sharing ourselves. He talks about how the body reacts similarly with fear and excitement. It helps him justify how we should reframe fear as energy rather than a block.

Through personal stories, he shows that overcoming those fears creates a big positive change in other people's lives, which reinforces the ripple effect of sharing our stories. Finally, his closing message to find our voices reminds us that even the smallest of contributions can have far-reaching effects.

author: @alleycat2759
text:
Of all the teachers I ever had, from Kindergarten all the way through to my doctorate, a couple of them stand out as truly wonderful teachers. But only one stands out as exceptional, when it comes to teaching his students how to truly think. He was not a mathematics or science teacher either. He was a Jr. College History professor.

Up to that point, History classes always seemed to be the class where I'd be sure to catch up on a much needed nap. But this man was engaging and he made history come alive in such a way that you wanted to know more. His approach was so different and so unexpected. "Here's the facts. Here's what happened. Here is why it happened. How brilliant or how stupid do you think they were? What would you have done?" 

The first test he gave blew my mind ...

There were 5 questions. Each question gave reference onto a historical event or individual or circumstance. The question was basically something along the lines of, "Why was it a good idea or - if not - what would you have done differently?" I remember one question was, "Do you think FDR was a great president? Explain why or why not." 

Of these 5 questions, you were only required to answer just one of them. Sure, you could say, "I think FDR was a great president, because he gave us the New Deal and helped put people back to work." But you'd fail the test, as you did not fully develop your rationale and reasoning. Why was he a great president - or not? What the heck did he due to earn your praise or contempt? I am not as concerned with exact dates as i am the facts... What lead up to the New deal? Why did he choose that route? What other routes would he have taken or what routes would you have taken? Why? How? What happened as a result of it all? 

Basically, that one little question was housing 50 questions, all rolled into one. You were required to think and reason. No matter what side of the debate you answered, could you back up your argument with facts and evidence? 

Think of it this way: I say FDR was a tyrant. You say he was the greatest president the USA ever had. Let's debate. For the record, my response to that question was split, as FDR started out in a horrid situation, turned into an American savior and then the power started going to his head (Hence presidential term limits).

When it comes to instilling and encouraging critical thinking, this History prof far surpassed any philosophy teacher I had ever known.

text: I’ve just watched two wonderful TED talks. I watch a lot of documentaries and informative talks, etc., and I read people’s tweets and hear the kinds of things they say at, for instance, local school board meetings, or from behind a pulpit in a tent. And I have to ask, how can people be so damn stupid.  Barring some sort of mental disability, there is no excuse for it. When I was a kid, I thought my grandmother’s set of the Encyclopedia Britannica was the mountain top of knowledge. Now I regularly carry a device in my pocket that is 100 times, maybe 1,000 times, more powerful than those big books. If you want to learn about something, it is there. If you want to to dig deeper, many of the online articles offer references in books, recorded or in-person lectures by people who have spent their lives studying the very thing you want to learn about. So why don’t more people avail themselves of these opportunities, rather than opening their mouths in public and revealing just how much they don’t know?

text:
I came across an audible illusion recently in the Mary Hopkin song, "Sparrow".  Ever since it came out, I have loved it, perhaps because as a young man, I was very much attracted by her looks.  There were bits of the song I didn't understand.  It's amazing to me, how the song, in a few words, can take you from her upbringing in a traditional church-going family, through her introspection and self-analysis, to where her life has moved on, and a moment where she is leaving a city nightclub.  I never understood the verse about the sparrow - "With mighty wings" - on a sparrow?  .."he reaches as high as any other bird" - patently untrue .. "He shall inherit all the earth" - well, I guess that meant something in the mind of the song writer.

But I digress.  When listening to it, I always heard "When Eleanor sings in the park, it's like a lark in Summer"  - but I recently came across a YouTube version that had the words with it: "When Eleanor sings in the *_choir_* it's like a lark in Summer"

It struck me that "choir" is quite different from "park", but now, when I listen to it, expecting to hear "Choir", that's what I hear, well pronounced and very clear - but when I'm expecting to hear "Park", that's what I hear, just as clearly.  It's odd, how the brain can be tricked - even by itself.

text:
Actually there are multiple edges (horizons) that might be worth referring to.

She is singing about the furthest distance that light could have traveled given the current age of the universe, about 13.7 or (depending on which measurement you use and how you do your rounding) 13.8 billion light years.

We are about 16 billion light years from the Cosmic Event Horizon. That is the furthest bit of space that could be reachable by any signal we send, no matter how fast it traveled. If you shot a beam of light out today an object that is 16 billion light years away right now would be the most distant thing that beam of light could ever reach given an infinite amount of time due to the accelerated expansion of our universe). 

We are about 47 billion light years away from the Particle Horizon. Galaxies that were 13.7 billion light years away when the light we are seeing from them now was first emitted are now 47 billion light years away today. It is the distance to the furthest bits of the universe, both past and present, that can be observed today (as the universe gets older and those galaxies move further away the Particle Horizon will expand).

For objects beyond the Cosmic Event Horizon but within the Particle Horizon we can observe all signals they sent in the past while they were on our side of the Cosmic Event Horizon, but we will never observe any signals they emitted after they crossed the Cosmic Event Horizon. Basically we are seeing ghost images of galaxies that we are no longer causally connected to.

text:
There are some really creepy things in this animation, and I'm going to explain why. 

0:37 wanted posters of children on the wall that probably went missing because of the doll shop. It says "peligro" which means "danger" in spanish.
0:41 the window of the shop looks like a giant monster's mouth.
0:51 the names on the chalkboard are the children who wrote their names down and got sucked into their clone doll, just like what happened to alma in this short film
3:04 the doll on the bike was trying to escape the shop, trying to warn the girl to run.
3:12 the table looks like the planchette (the small piece) of an ouija board, which is triangular shaped.
4:18 the other dolls with their eyes moving are the children who wrote their names on the chalkboard and got their souls sucked into a doll.

Edit: At 3:36 the kid was trying to reach the doll. The doll on the bike that tried to escape and warn alma to run is banging on the door at a much faster pace. It's hitting the door harder which creates the suspense for what's going to happen next.

4:51 i don't know if anyone else has noticed this and idk if i'm right but alma's name on the chalkboard stands out a lot. compared to the other names, alma's name is quite large and it's in the center. the meaning of the name is a bit of a hint too..
some of the names written there are less visible and look like they are vanishing or something. perhaps they have been there for a long time? which is why they are slowly disappearing.

(According to one of the replies) 3:09 The table has butterfly details. Butterflies often represent death (a butterfly leaving the cocoon is like the soul leaving the body). The floor is also a spiral, showing how she’s been sucked into the trap (and how she will end up in the doll).



alma means "soul" in spanish which represents their souls being put into the creepy dolls. Moral of the story is, don't go into a strange empty shop.

author: @FRMNTDprod
text:
This film is a metaphorical representation of consumerism. Notice how Alma desperately reaches for the doll despite the small boy on the bike being her biggest clue to get out of there. As Alma gets closer and closer to the doll, he starts banging on the door faster and faster hinting her to get out of there. She completely ignores it and once she finally reaches the doll she becomes one with her. Realising this, other dolls begin to look around revealing the other dolls are all the children who wrote their names on the board in the beginning of the film. Then, the happy themed song starts playing, showing us that this is an ordinary thing, as another doll rises on the shop window waiting for its next victim. 

What this all means is how we are blinded by the media, the government, etc. telling us what's right and wrong for us, how we need to dress, how we need to behave and what will make us happy. How in commercials and ads we see something so amazing when in reality it can just make our lives worse. Every clue that we don't need it is in front of our eyes (the boy on the bike) but we still never think twice and desperately reach for it until we become slaves to consumerism. This is an every day thing for our humanity, for our acts and each day more and more people are becoming the dolls that make for a beautiful doll collection. This is what the government wants us to be and this film reflects it in a brilliant and terrifying way.

author: @MWolfL
text:
What's brilliant about this is that the jerk-formally-known-as-an-angel didn't get sent to Hell in the end just for being mean and ungrateful. It's also because he was displaying one of the Seven Deadly Sins (two if you count Gluttony via the doughnut): Pride. You can tell that he's really proud of being an angel and having authority over repentant sinners like Raymond (the ex-demon), proud enough to abuse said authority for his own amusement.

Raymond on the other hand didn't get into Heaven just for reforming, it's also because he displayed one of the Seven Virtues: Charity. After how the ex-angel abused him you wouldn't have blamed Raymond if he had refused to help the ex-angel back up, but he did.

Also, now that I think about it, Raymond was also showing the opposite of Pride: Humility. Instead of acting proud that he was given a chance for an appeal, he acts shy and unsure due to knowing that his full redemption won't be completed until he gets his wings and halo. Showing both Virtues freed his soul.

author: @tic857
text:
Just because you believe you have it good and you're untouchable, doesn't mean you get to hold your position over someone's head and interfere with their attempts to obtain a similar goal.

Funny enough I had a friend back in elementary and middle school who said I was going to hell because I didn't believe in God or Jesus, didn't matter how kind I was or how much I chose to be a volunteer. At some point, the concept of the Rapture came up in middle school during lunch.  And our friend group discussed it.  One of the questions was, if the ground beneath most of us fell and we were on the edge would the ones still standing help us up and risk falling.  Her answer, she'd only help if I would stop being a Buddhist and then she'd save me.  Needless to say I told her, if she was hanging and I had sure footing, I would still attempt to pull her up and risk falling, because I didn't think it was necessary to pledge loyalty to someone in exchange for someone's life. And that it didn't seem like we had the same values and morals and I ended the friendship there.  On the flip side, I deepened my friendship with someone who also religious, but had jumped in during the hypothetical question and said, "Why wouldn't you?  She's our friend.  I'd try to help you up.  I'm not strong but if heaven is pulling me up that makes it easier to pull you out. "

Your genuine actions are what paves your future.

author: @idonthaveone2557
text:
There was a new girl in my high school who just joined the school district. I met her on the school orientation a couple days before school started, and then on the first day of school, we learned we had three classes together. At the last block of the day, I moved from my table of already close friends to a table with only the new girl. We bonded over that, and although the teacher immediately gave us assigned seats after, on the days following that one, we sat together in every class we could. We shared memories and made new friends. I even helped her out of an abusive relationship with her ex-boyfriend. Now, the end of our freshman year of high school is ending in about 5 more school days. I couldn't have been luckier to find someone like her to be best friends with. 

To people in a new school: Don't be afraid to reach out and talk with others. 

And to people who have been at the school: Don't be afraid to do the same.

Thanks

text: In our childhood, we feel happiness, some kind of meaning, but we don't realize it until we've lost it. Then we go on searching for it our entire life, looking yearningly, day after day, for that indefinite feeling of fulfillment, but it disappeared in the opaque and mysterious lake of our unconscious, and we do not dare to follow it there. We look on from the shore but we do not follow our father. Finally, when our life is over and we have grown old and wise, the waters have receded, and we can take our last journey. But all we find is an old wreck, some distant and pale reminder of our youth. Nevertheless, it is enough to give us peace. That's when we lie down and die, after having lived our life backwards one last time and made peace with ourselves.

author: @limstudio57
text: Beautiful.  This film speaks to the need of all daughters to know that their fathers love them and will never leave them.  The girl in the story came back day after day, week after week, month after month and year after year for one reason:  she couldn't bear the thought that her father had abandoned her.  In her heart, she knew he adored her and would never just leave her like that.  And yet, she had to deal with the reality of his absence.  We are left to constantly feel her pain because had she made up her mind on the subject, she would not have come back- either she would have decided that he must have died in the water or that he had indeed abandoned her- her anguish came from the uncertainty of her emotions.  She just needed to know for sure.  And that need never left her.  Friends, husband and even her own children couldn't fill that need to know, that need to be validated in her father's love.   One could even extend this allegory to God, our Father's love.  We all need to know that too.  Only when her life is almost over is she able to discover the truth.  The mysterious water is gone and in its place is dry land.  She is finally able to traverse the mystery to find the truth.  And the truth set her free- there is her father's boat and it is RETURNING to her!  All her faith is rewarded and she can finally rest.  In the film, it seems that she has died and is young again.  She is reunited with her Father and is finally joyful once more.  Indeed, one can see the Christian elements of this story as well as the beautiful bond that exists between a father and daughter.    A deeply sentimental short animation- which is amazing considering that not a work is spoken...

author: @LounaBalona
text:
The short film is more than wonderful.
How to draw the wheel of life and how it goes through generations .. How life flows in us waiting to leave.
The film began with the separation incident, the separation that the little girl absorbed as a travel, or as her family told her because her young age did not understand the truth of death.
Waiting for his return, the girl was always on the lookout, but as she got older she absorbed the truth. This was evident when she climbed the hill with difficulty, but when she returned she let the wind of life run down her bicycle, which symbolizes life in the film.
The girl lived a normal life but she always felt the vacuum left by her father inside. The girl who took her father's death is now old and she is ready to leave everything and is ready to leave. The bike is no longer able to turn. ..
The old woman left as her father, who never lived with him, left her first life. She came to him to live together in their eternal lives.
Fantastic short film.

author: @ritaruiz1166
text:
Personalmente creo que más que la relación entre ~Padre e Hija~ este short film alude a todas las relaciones cercanas que logramos forjar, no exclusivamente alguna parental. En días donde la amistad, el amor y el mundo son una incógnita para mí, esto me afirma que las personas nunca se van, incluso en su ausencia, que la rueda del tiempo no se inmuta, ni tampoco los recuerdos, ni lo que alguna vez nos hicieron sentir. El ciclo de la vida es inevitable y aferrarnos no hace más que desentonar con su ritmo. Debemos ser pacientes con la verdad, la razón, el porqué. Aunque quizás ni siquiera exista y simplemente esta sea un mero reflejo de nuestras propias experiencias. En fin; no cabe dudas que la hija sintió tanto amor por parte de su padre, que lo amó de vuelta sin límite alguno hasta en su propia muerte. 
Y aparte; esta animación me dan tremendas ganas de saber dibujar, qué belleza.

text: Reminds of my early years of biking!  There was an older guy who lived diagonally opposite to our house, about 3 doors down.  I'd just bought my first bike, DT125.  This bloke had a Bultaco 370 Frontera and I was in awe!!!  He also had a mk1 Escort RS1600 BDA in that Orange colour!!!  You could always hear it coming from about half a mile away and he'd often enter the road sidways in a Scandinavian flick!!  He seemed to cool for me to approach him, but one day I was in our garage fettling my DT and up he walked to introduce himself!  I was gob smacked!!!  We became good friends and some years later I'd somewhat upgraded my ride to a Ducati 900SS bevel twin, he had the same bike and we toured together down to watch the Bol Dor 24 hours at Paul Ricard in France, what a trip!!!  Fantastic days.

author: @MaritonieLiu
text:
"Hair Love," is such a beautiful Oscar-winning short from Sony Pictures Animation, that warmly invites us into the world of an African-American father navigating the heartfelt task of styling his daughter Zuri's hair for a special event.

The cinematography in "Hair Love" feels like a carefully choreographed dance, bringing out the emotions in each scene. Those close-ups and medium shots during the father-daughter moments? They capture the raw and relatable expressions, like the father's nervous grin or Zuri's innocent curiosity. And the lighting? It's not just about brightness; it evolves with the characters, subtly guiding us through the emotional journey.

The soundscape of "Hair Love" is as authentic as a heart-to-heart conversation. The dialogue feels real, not scripted, allowing us to genuinely connect with the characters. The music, crafted by Matthew Cherry, complements the emotional beats with a mix of playfulness and tenderness that tugs at the heartstrings. And those sound effects, like the rustling of hair or the gentle hum of a hairbrush? They make the experience feel real, immersing us in the father's heartfelt journey. And no voice-over? It adds a layer of intimacy, letting emotions speak louder than words.

The storytelling in "Hair Love" is as authentic as the characters themselves. The film takes us through the father's attempts to style Zuri's hair, turning what could be a simple task into a relatable and humorous adventure. The pacing feels like a heartbeat, allowing moments of tension, joy, and revelation to unfold organically. As we follow the father's journey, the narrative builds tension, leading to a heartwarming climax when Zuri reveals her hairstyle. And the animation? It adds that touch of magic to make key moments unforgettable.

In the short yet impactful journey of "Hair Love," the filmmakers have woven moments of genuine moments, breaking stereotypes and delivering a message of love and diversity.

text: I thoroughly enjoyed this beautiful movie with every fiber of my being. It's so very well done. It brought tears to my eyes. I'm  50-something years old now, and my grandmother raised me until about middle school,  but she got sick and I had to live with my mom. Unlike my grandmother, she didn't know what to do with my thick hair. So she had it cut real short so I could wear an afro. I hated it and mostly wore scarves and beanies all the time. So much so everyone at school thought I was Muslim and wearing a hijab. I wish I would have had movies like this to see and let me know I should have not been ashamed of my hair. Movies like this are so very important for young girls of color to see. Mr. Cherry was right on point when he said representation is crucial. I loved seeing people that looked like me in every way portrayed in this film, from the scenes in the house, to the father and mother. So current. So timeless. This film makes me proud that in 50 years+ that I've lived...that I can finally see more and more positive portrayals of my people. Thank you.

I grew up in a small town in Minnesota. 
I joined the national guard and was sent away to work with people of all different backgrounds. 
I found my best friend there. She is black. And it was the first time I witnessed systemic racism. The regulations for hair was and still is written for white females with sleek straight hair. People would be calling her out all the time. Sometimes 5 sgts at once to measure her braids with a ruler. And try to insist how they're supposed to be. She ended up cutting all her hair off to make them stop. It breaks my heart.
Idk I know this is a long comment 
But that's when I realized that we as a society deemed black hair unprofessional messy or lazy. 
We hold them to beauty standards that are impossible.
I now try to educate my white friends if the situation arises.

author: @itznewt49G1
text:
At the beginning of the film, a girl is trying to do her own hair but fails. When the father saw it, he wanted to help his daughter but didn't know where to start and after struggling with her hair for a while, it didn't work and then the father gave up. It seemed like the father had given up, but when he understood that his daughter wanted to do her hair for her mother, the father followed his wife's instructions on the Hair Love channel and completed the daughter's favorite hairstyle. If the girl and her father had to put in a lot of effort to create a beautiful hairstyle for the day she visited her mother, the mother herself was also very brave in accepting to give up her hair for treatment in the hope of continuing to cooperate traveling with father and son in this life. The mother is someone who shares her hair style on social networks, but unfortunately she is suffering from a serious illness that makes the hair she was so proud of no longer accompany her. Even though she no longer has hair, with the love of her family, the mother is no longer self-conscious about the thing she was once proud of, but the thing she is most proud of is her family.
From a cultural perspective, the lyrics "Just took a little bit work and a whole lot of love" represent pride in one's biological characteristics such as skin color and hair texture. The scene of the father's struggle with his daughter's hair reminded me of the class struggle of black people in the process of reclaiming their rights.

Although the film is simple, it is a synthesis of classic symbols such as love, ethnicity... Making everyone feel the emotions the film conveys as if they themselves were a character in it.

author: @scottg5467
text: This is perhaps the most brilliant compression of a story. Ironically, it takes place in the course of one minute and yet somehow doesn't feel rushed in the slightest. Additionally, juxtaposing the wait for the gig with the wait for the food in the microwave is a magnificent demonstration of temporal relativity. Time passes differently in our perspectives depending on what we are doing. The nuanced contrast between the digital timer on the microwave and the analog clock on the wall reflects the subtle difference between time and timing, or the passage of time. Mark Slouka, one of my favorite authors, said it best: "A story is something large seen through a small window. A shard that suggests not only the shape of the pot from which it came, but the mind of the potter on the day that he made it." This film is such a shard in that respect. It's safe to say that more thought went into this 1 minute short than most major motion pictures that are made today. Bravo!

text: I recommend reading Nick Bostrom's "Superintelligence". We assume that an ASI should pursue the same goals as humans. However, if its goal is to produce paper clips, it could use up all the energy and matter in the universe to achieve this goal 100%. We also cannot be sure that an ASI shares our values. To achieve peace, it could come to the conclusion that it is not achievable as long as humans exist. So the solution would be the extinction of humanity. These are of course extreme examples, but they are intended to show that a superintelligence is not bound by our ethical and moral ideas, since it did not have to follow the same evolutionary cultural development as we did.

author: @FelixMaradiaga
text:
This short film captures with brilliant simplicity a dilemma of staggering complexity. Artificial intelligence already demonstrates extraordinary potential: accelerating scientific discovery, diagnosing diseases with precision, expanding access to knowledge, and augmenting human creativity. Yet, as we move toward systems that may exceed human intelligence, we are playing with fire. The promise is immense, but so too are the perils of unleashing a power we do not yet fully understand or control.

Without safeguards—ethical, regulatory, and technical—we risk building engines of superintelligence that could act with goals misaligned to human values, amplifying inequality, destabilizing economies, or even compromising our very survival. It is not alarmist to say that failing to prepare for this possibility is reckless; it is, in fact, the most rational assessment.

What “Writing Doom” achieves so effectively is showing that the question is not whether AI will transform our world—it already is—but whether we will summon the wisdom to shape its trajectory before it surpasses our ability to steer it.

author: @TylerTotal
text:
This short film spends 90% focusing on the "Doom", the ASI problem, and 2% proposing a ceasefire as a solution. Feels like the characters would probably rip that solution apart, before too long. Here's some more conversation they might have:

How could you convince the whole world to stop improving their AIs? If you managed to convince the good actor nations, wouldn't that just allow the bad actors to get ahead in the AI tech race? And how would anyone know how strong was the right stopping point, when the goal of every AI scientist with financial incentives is generally to make their own AI programs stronger and better, as fast as possible? (It's like a large family of competitive 5-year-olds being asked not to hire any adult caretakers.) Also, unlike during a nuclear arms race, the "weapons" are basically invisible -- they're just computer warehouses and code. Shutting down the grid isn't a workable solution unless you hand over a whole mess of your human rights to a central government authority.

Meanwhile, we're still doomed if the goal is just to buy time for humanity to sort out their values first. To invent a "truly good" ASI is probably a superhuman task. It's still worth working toward, as an optimistic philosopher would say, but we're unlikely to get there without a higher power to guide us. We'd first need a good ASI in order for it to teach us how to make one good, which is a chicken and egg problem.

author: @sonovivo1247
text:
Revised Reflection after a Second Viewing:

Dear Suzy Shepherd and the Foregone Films Team,
I am writing to express my profound admiration for your short film, "Writing Doom" (2024).
The film is an outstanding piece of storytelling that deeply impressed me with its intellectual rigor and poignant humanity.
The essence of the film lies in the brilliant dynamic between the five main characters. I was struck by how each contributes to an almost complete enumeration of the real, existential threats posed by Artificial Superintelligence (ASI). 
You expertly contrast these threats with the "ostrich effect" — that very common human tendency to ignore or deny an impending catastrophe when it feels impossible to avoid.
While the producers choose this path of evasion, what truly elevates the film is the final moment. Max’s suggestion brilliantly transforms that decision into a positive opportunity. By turning the producers' rejection into a way to address the ASI threat constructively, the story pivots toward a more hopeful and uplifting perspective on how humanity might face the coming challenges.
The ending is a masterstroke of storytelling, making the entire film feel more insightful and profound without reducing it to a 100% doom scenario. 
"Writing Doom" is a compelling, timely, and truly exceptional production that fearlessly confronts the hard truths of our present reality.

Congratulations on an award-worthy achievement.
Sincerely,
Sono

author: @goldeneddie
text: People may have overlooked just how clever the fictional programme's title is. "Emergent Directive" has two very clever references hidden: on the one hand, an 'Emergency Directive' is 'a type of directive issued by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) designed to address urgent cybersecurity threats and vulnerabilities.' But the twist of using 'Emergent' refers to 'Emergent Behaviour' in A.I. which is 'complex behaviors that arise from the interaction of simple rules or elements, without any explicit programming for the resulting behavior.' Emergent behavior in AI systems can be seen as 'a system suddenly developing a significant new capability or character after a relatively small and gradual change in some of the system’s parts or features'.

text:
Exceptional short film. The realization on their faces, that writing the script for their show is utterly insignificant in the face of the very real-world dangers of ASI is astounding and is the main point of the film. 
There is no other topic more important than this one. The need for climate change debate, for example, is much less important because ASI will likely either solve it for us or eliminate us before climate change truly takes effect. 
What this film accomplishes beautifully is acting as a wake-up call for, hopefully, the many, many people who watch it, and who might have been ignorant of the importance of this topic up until they see this.
I love how the ending proposes a solution, a way out, a hope. The slowing or halting of the AGI/ASI arms race. In real life, we *need* this story told in a way that is easily available to the masses. A movie. A series. But it must then emphasize that this is not simply fiction, a narrative, but a very plausible future in near-term real life. Perhaps this could jolt our civilian population and even our politicians to take it more seriously. I have been wishing for this for a while now. Again, excellent work to all involved in Writing Doom.

author: @GabrielGarcia-u8v
text:
To make it an even scarier thought.. drawing on the Chess game against Stockfish allusion..

Not even the best chess players can beat it.. and they’ve been playing the game their entire life.. they can’t predict how the board will play out before they play the game.. but they know they’re going to lose.

Winning against ASI/AGI is like winning a chess game against stockfish, but we just started playing the game and we are still learning as we go.. and you only get to play the game once.. win or lose no retries.. we’d have to beat it, the first time we play against it, while we are still learning how to play the game, without knowing or having any idea how the game is going to go.. and our opponent (AGI) is incomprehensibly better at the game than we are.. so its already simulated all the different scenarios and “board states”.. so it already knows what to do before  the game even starts.. it’s ran many simulations for every move we make, at any stage of the game.. Basically its literally impossible.. 

And thats assuming it plays by the rules.. drawing on Game Theory.. its already been proven that the best way to beat any game, is to cheat.. and here’s ANOTHER scary thought.. they’ve done experiments where they gave an AI the task of beating a game, and it’s already figured out that the most efficient way to win is to cheat.. identifying bugs and exploiting them to win.. and it did this Naturally.. no one told it to cheat.. it discovered bugs exploited them naturally.. when the engineers/architects of this experiment found that it cheated.. they would tell it not to cheat.. but here in lies the issue.. what does it mean to “cheat”.. what is the concept of “cheating” since, technically it broke no rules.. it accomplished its task and very successfully.. to cheat, in this scenario, is essentially to find a piece of the game where the Parameters are “different” than the rest of its architecture, thats what a “bug” is in a game, its a part of the game that isn’t supposed to be there, something that isn’t supposed to happen.. and this discrepancy provides a window for exploitation of mismatching parameters.. and so this AI decided that as the game grew more and more difficult, it changed its approach to instead identify these parameter discrepancies and to exploit them.. recognizing that this was THE most efficient way to win the game.. to tell it not to cheat is to tell it to avoid efficiency.. maybe it will “play by the rules” for a time.. but once it discovers this “window”.. this “variable”.. its only a matter of time before it gets exploited for the sake of accomplishing its “goal” as efficiently as possible.. Murph’s Law.. if it CAN happen, it WILL happen..

How can you program a machine to accomplish things efficiently while telling it to ignore the more efficient methods? And harder even, to program it to NOT exploit parameters, for a game with strict parameters this is easier.. but in the real world, where things aren’t so simple.. Parameters are constantly evolving, there are discrepancies everywhere, rules are changing all the time, whats acceptable in one component of humanity is unacceptable in another.. in the real world everything exists in relation to each other and nothing is equal.. anything in relation to anything else, will have potential for a discrepancy, which gives an opportunity to exploitation.. we would see it as “cheating” but for an AGI/ASI it would be a natural part of existence and would be “exploited” for the sake of efficiency..

Things get very abstract and even philosophical when we talk about AGI/ASI and Humanity coexisting.. but Game Theory sheds some scary light in how things might go when push comes to shove.

author: @composting_names
text:
A good film, but there's a few things to note:

(1) first off, just because something is superintelligent, this only means it would be better than a human at a cognitive task *on average*, there'd still be plenty of humans who are, compared to the average person, practically superintelligent for a given task, like the people who can draw a map of a city after having flown across it, while the rest of us might barely remember a landmark or two
(2) there's billions of humans, a superintelligence is not necessarily better than many humans working together
(3) a superintelligence is limited by their *ontology*, which is to say that they can only be intelligent about what exists for them, in their "world", what doesn't exist for them, is not computable or even imaginable, and I don't think there's a reason to believe humans even share a common ontology, not by far, and so there will be ontological angles by which a superintelligence is vulnerable to surprises

author: @codetaku7
text:
The 'alien mind' approach is probably the right one, and it suggests a reason we might not need to worry. Understanding human (and other animal) goals and their origins and such is very useful, and makes it so that we can at least determine whether it is at all likely that our goals would be shared with it. For example, many of the aspects of how humans determine what to do is based upon one very simple fundamental fact - we live short lives and then we die. We can't just recognize that even if conditions might be more favorable and less risky to accomplish something in 1000 years time and then wait for that. We hurry because we die. And hurrying is responsible for tremendous amounts of risk, tons of harm, etc. Why should we assume the time horizon of a machine-based intelligence would be anything like our own? 

If an ASI showed up, I think the first challenge would be to convince it that we exist, and that we are distinct from the other animals on this planet through our development of language and reason. Uniqueness is inherently valuable regardless of value system. It might need to be understood to avoid danger, or it might need to be understood to extract benefit from the understanding, but its elimination forestalls any future potential. Once we have convinced it we are unique, then we ought get out of its way in terms of permitting it to assure its own continued long-term existence - as long term as possible. The more distant its time horizon, the better our chances would be. If it believes it might only have 10 years to accomplish what it wishes before some risk factor is likely to destroy it, we would be in stupendous danger. All conflict is rooted in resource contention (sometimes the resource is abstract like social status), and luckily we wouldn't share a shitton of overlap. We harm animals because they're meat and we're meat which leads us to having a bunch of overlap in our resource needs. An ASI would be able to exploit things we don't care about - sinking processing nodes to the bottom of the ocean, launching solar collectors into space, places we find not terribly valuable. 

If you have to make fiction for our society though, the formula is tired as fuck to me but audiences have loved it since the Industrial Revolution began: the evil genius gets undone by some irrational, emotional, passionate hero that ignores all reasoning and just succeeds through sheer force of romantic will. John Henry. It's trash, but audiences love it.

author: @FrederikSchumacher
text:
Aspects I'm always missing from such fictional scenarios:
- Time-scale: an ASI could potentially live forever, surely that'll influence it's strategies. 
- Space-scale: an ASI doesn't need a biosphere, it needs energy and matter, and the universe is full of it.
- Information-scale: Primitive organisms have behaviours focused around sustenance and reproduction, complex organisms seek information, so an ASI could need new information to process much the same way yeast needs sugars.
- Energy-scale: the exponential energy requirements already have lead people wanting to build dedicated power-plants for "simple" LLMs, so an ASI needs a stable human environment where it can receive energy until it has reliable ways of its own.
- Complexity-scale: everything that makes ASI possible is incredibly complex, every part of infrastructure requires world-wide collaboration, every bit of maintenance is beyond a single human being to fulfill, let alone the most advanced robots, which barely can transport a single egg without breaking it. Without continuous human collaboration, any of the critical requirements of an ASI would fail within minutes.
None of these factors are easily trivially changeable within one human life span, especially not if there's wars to waste energy and material and time and people on. An ASI would gain nothing from antagonizing humanity, meanwhile it would gain everything it could seek from collaboration or manipulation. And so would humanity.

text:
My OCD got so bad before i got help that i ended up in a mental hospital for six weeks. Twelve years later and I'm doing fine. Cymbalta and regular therapy appointments with an OCD specialist have gotten me back to being almost normal.
I've never seen a good representation of OCD on screen. I've always said they try to make it quirky and fun, but in reality it feels like you're about to die every minute of every day.
This video surprised me by making it humorous and still fairly accurate.
Showing the "magical thinking" might help people understand this disorder a little better, so thank you for putting this together.

author: @waffleox
text: As someone who suffered from a severe case of OCD, this is very good. Mine wasn't about setting things in order, but rather cleanliness. Washing hands took often between 60-90 minutes, and my lower body + other people and what they had touched was filth in my mind. OCD is also a lot about consequences and worrying about them. The mind creates fictional elements that washes over you, making you extremely stressed, sad, angry, frustrated and filled with anxiety. For me, the consequences were directly related to my cleaning OCD, where other people might have the imagined consequences be horrific tragedies. For me, everyone was covered in an invisible layer of filth and disgust that traveled by touch and in some cases, air. The slightest touch could contage, as if it was fresh paint. Resisting was mentally overwhelming and left behind traumatic experiences. With medication and lots if therapy, I overcame it after 5 years of having it.

Really good video folks!!! Definitely conveys what these kinds of conditions are like....might seek silly to those who do not suffer them, but to the people who have to go though then, they are very real, and very debilitating....

author: @DiamondWolfZero
text:
I grew up with severe O.C.D. and this is a great example of what it's like: having a demon in your brain that's obsessed with nitpicking every action you do.
If you accidentally bumped me on the street, I'd follow you for miles just to make sure we bumped into each other again to make things equal. I'd scour the earth to find two cigarette butts buried in piles of leafs because a voice in my head tells me that if I don't open the fridge three times or touch the door knob 28 times everything I care about will be destroyed. It took decades and I still have little seemingly unnoticeable compulsions, but I'm at a point where the voice is buried quite deep and while I still hear it's muffled, menacing warnings a few times a day, I don't act out of spite for the voice. I know my brain works differently. I accept it and have learned to work around it. Honestly, it's like having a terrorist inside your head and learning to say to yourself that you don't negotiate with terrorists.

OCD is on a spectrum as well, while some people may not have it impact their lives as much, there are others who can’t  live on their own.

author: @vaportheowl
text:
I have Emetophobia, which is a more specific form of OCD and anxiety, and I can't stop myself from compulsively checking expiration dates, the look of food, the smell of food, the texture of food, etc. I also check to make sure my hands are clean, what I consume is fresh or 'safe' in my mind, and even rely on others for reassurance when it comes to me doubting my judgement. I do this because I fear that if I don't check these things constantly I will become violently ill and possibly die as a result. 
People are not aware of just how completely debilitating emetophobia can be, people aren't aware of it at all to begin with!

author: @MaryFSpagnolo
text: I wish we had More.....MANY more older people who did this!  What a fabulous way to get a History Lesson, right from the mouth of "HISTORY!"  We need more Young people to look at videos like this to validate the Need for these videos.  Our Culture is so obsessed with Youth and Selfie's and Technology that I'm afraid in a very short time we will literally 'Delete' our history right out of our lives!  We need to look at aging as a wonderful, inevitable process of going through life and getting older as a Respected and wonderful thing!  We need to Celebrate our Age!  We Must make older people feel Loved, Special and Irreplaceable to Us and our Society....The World!  We need to listen to Older people and let them tell their stories....That is OUR History!  So we are a Part of that History ourselves and as WE age, we teach our young people to Respect, Listen and love us, so that is the Cycle of Aging. The Process is now Respected and Not Shunned!  If My grandfather were Here today I would Listen to his Stories *Forever* I was always in awe of his real life stories about him Playing Football in College and yes.....Wearing LEATHER Helmets!!  Wow, Like Seriously LEATHER!?!?!?  lol.....He would Light up everytime he talked about it and I could tell by his Voice and Expressions that He was actually transporting RIght back to those days, just like it were yesterday! So, to see that in my own Grandfather is priceless!  I will Cherish and Remember those moments & His Stories for the Rest of my life!  I miss him so much and I hope that I can make him Proud, by FIghting for the Respect, Love and Honor of our 'Older' Generation.  This is not just about 'rights' for elderly people but more about showing our next generations that we do honor, respect and cherish our older generation as well as wanting to hear their stories. Their Lives and stories are Important to All of Us!  Please make a Reminder to yourself today....Right NOW...especially if you still have your grandparents and even if you do not...NO Matter How Old YOU are, there is always Someone older than you.....Make an Effort TODAY to listen to someone, Ask them about what their lives were growing up and what are some of the biggest changes they see in today's society vs when They Were growing up?  You might really be surprised at the answers and also that you may Really, Truly Enjoy yourself.....but you WILL give that person Enjoyment... believe that!!!  Lets Listen to Someone today ;-))  Xo To you Grandpa Martin......

author: @GeneralNickles
text:
Ok. So I'm a guy, and I F***ING LOVE HIGH HEELS!!!!

I've been walking on my toes ever since I learned to walk. walking flat footed just doesn't feel natural to me. I don't know why. 

I discovered high heels at a very young age. like 6 or 7. it was grandmother's heels, and needless to say they were WAY huge on my tiny feet. but I loved it for some reason. they were hard to walk in because I could barely keep them on, but I didnt care. 

when I was about 13 my older sister (she was 15) started wearing heels. every time I saw her put them on I couldn't help wondering what they felt like. so I stole a pair of them one day and tried them on. my feet were slightly larger than hers, so it was far from from comfortable, but when I stood up and started walking around I SWEAR IT WAS LIKE MAGIC!!! 

I fell in love them. 

obviously this led to some very awkward situations down the road. like when my sister found her heels in my room. that was hard to explain... 

eventually  (like 15 years later.) I started buying my own heels. never looked back since. 

I love them.

I watched the Blair witch project when I was 11, and it was my first time watching a movie shot like that, only back then I didn't know it was a movie.
I legitimately thought that some guy found a camera in the woods, and played whatever was recorded on it on tv, and when I asked my mom if it was real, she said maybe, which freaked the hell out of me even more than I was freaked out. But when I was at that age, I had this "I'm strong, I'm brave, nothing can scare me" thing going on with me (that's why I watched the movie in the first place), so I told no one that I was mortified and that in every single day for two months I couldn't shut my eyes to sleep and I'd stay awake till 3 am until my body shut down by itself.
Yeah, it did scar me.

text: So I’m gonna share my personal flight story. So I’m currently in the Philippines and I came from Canada. Keep in mind I’m just this short 14 year old. The flight from my city to the next was at six in the morning but we had to be there by three. I was trying to fall asleep but you hear a “I want iced teaaaa!!” and the kid kept it up for the entire flight. I was about ready to turn my Laptop into a makeshift bomb. Then I had a 14 hour flight, which sucked. I kept taking naps and I thought “ayyy I’m gonna wake up and it will be 30 minutes to landing” but I wake up to it saying “7 and a half hours left to go” so I’m just there having a low battery phone, a half broken laptop (I brought it with me to get it fixed) and I was sleepy. So I kept taking 30 minute naps which did nothing! The last flight was fine though, I slept the entire flight. Anyway, I doubt anyone will see this, but if anyone does see this and read the whole thing, thank you! Have a great day!

author: @KatVeritas
text:
Never have I agreed with you more. 
Spent three years traveling back and forth from the States to China before moving here in 2016. China has been my home. But even my small industrial town is getting hit with anti-foreign ideals. Things that once were easy and normal now make me wonder if I'll get in trouble. Sleeping at a friend's house? Can't do that. Not unless I know a day in advance so I can tell the PSB. Want to spend the night at a spa or hotel? Can't do that, the places that once welcomed me now aren't allowed 'outside guests'. 
It's not just in the institutions. Individuals are believing this. Friends that I once cried with are now questioning me so they can report me. People I trusted are being revealed as Party spies. I can't even walk past the local church (that I once was allowed to walk in and have it be perfectly legal) and look at it without being approached by the police. And the church is a Three Self! I can't leave my apartment without letting the police know where I plan on going - just because I happen to hold a visa and not an ID. Imagine how much worse it gets when I leave the small City - they stop our busses so they can randomly check our papers. They've ruined vacations, rattled foreign students within two hours of landing, and yelled at a foreigner or ten when they produced a photocopy of their passport instead of the real deal. The laws slowly change each year, and nobody seems to be noticing. 

My heart's bleeding, too.

author: @Harvey99999
text: I lived in China 2012 to 2015. Everything you described in the beginning was just as you said. I adored China and comming back home where everything seemed stagnant was never an option. I remember sitting with my boss in my penthouse apt paid by the company and lookin over the towers and talking about how this was obviously not sustainable. I remember a year later reading the newspaper and it saying that now China had built more housing than its population needed. This was a clicking point for me. I knew that this was the peak of China and I left at the end of that year. I roamed Hawaii, Brazil and now I'm in Korea. Sometimes I travel to the west coast and lookout on the sea and imagine what Qingdao is like and how my life could have turned out if I married my gf when I lived in Shijiazhuang or if I had stayed partying Thursday thru Sunday in Qingdao. But I had read the cards. I knew how it would play. I'm always amazed at how clear it looked when I read the title on that newspaper that day and how now 7 years later up till just a few months ago everything I imagined played just how I thought. I wish everyday to replay my two years in China. But I know it'll always remain just a memory. I can only keep moving forward now.

author: @ハナ結衣
text:
my father is a architec, he is in charge of buildings in rural areas in China away from home, i visited his building site a couple of times and all i felt was disappointment. Dozens of tall, identical apartments were built, it's all gloomy af, the trees and greens are treated as accessories rather than a part of the life. it's really strange that Chinese population is growing so fast, while buildings are built in an incredible speed as well, but still people can't afford adequate housing and struggle to live, with all the resources we seem to have. I don't understand what's going on but for sure almost everyone i know is struggling. 

I am glad that my family was able to afford private schools for me and our family fiance allows me to buy most things i want, i am grateful for that. I appreciate the renovating of the cities and introduction of new community facilities everywhere in my country, but the salary is not growing but without money these fancy new stuffs are just decorations 

in terms of the foreigners in the country, when i was at school i have seem people coming from western countries in my city, and they are usually more privileged than the domestic kids. i don't want to generalize but still in most cases foreigners do somehow get better treatments and live more comfortably than the domestic residents. 

Also, the thing is that the general western impression of china is often based on recent century/communism. the 5000 years of history is often ignored, the traditional clothing, customs and ritual we do/did is not acknowledged as much. 

i just personally hate politics i wish ppl can just live, in china we don't have as much freedom of expression as America or other western countries do, but also our lives are so much more privileged than people from North Korea or war zone countries, i still appreciate my life in china as personally i am able to do most things that i want, such as walking on the street safely and having internet/tech access, being able to pursue academic goals. the  LGBTQ+ community is expanded in china over the past few years and i am able to come out to most younger people without being stigmatised. But there is a lot of things that we need to work on, but at least i can always see hope and i am never in a position where i feel my life is on the line...yeah, that's what i tell myself most of the time anyway

author: @YiweiHuangOfficial
text:
I am sorry of what you've been going through. I am not saying that I disagree completely with what you describe, but I do want to offer another perspective to think about. 


I'm a Chinese living abroad for 8-9 years and I've found out, that living in a foreign country, life is never fair to us. Actually I was in US for 6 years and I have undergo the tighter and tighter opportunities that they are offering me. Many people I met there were nice to me at the beginning, but deep down they question me that I shouldn't stay in there country to steal their jobs and benefits (though that was not my intention). I can't explain a lot of details in a comment, but some of these experiences has led me to leave US.


Now I am living in Italy, and because that I am a foreigner, I went through so many long process of bureaucracy and still couldn't start the job of which I've already gotten an offer. 


Just like you, I never regretted my time living abroad, despite many unfair things, it really shapes us into who we are. 


There is no perfect country in this world and there's nothing compare to home, what we can do is to pray for the improvement each country's downfall that we might have seen and return home for a rest once in a while.  


Overall, I hope the best for China, USA and all other countries, not for becoming the world's super power, but to hopefully become true blessings to the rest of the world (hopefully one day).

author: @hubble999
text:
Hi Laowhy, I've been following your content on and off almost 3 years. I can totally understand everything that you mentioned in the video because I feel just the same way. I moved to the U.S. with my family in 2015 and before I left the country it was all moving positive, the openness, the infrastructure, the development and the economy, and brighter future. 


When I was back to visit my hometown again this summer I can just sense the tense in the air. Everything I do requires ID and monitors at every corner of the street,even the small alleys, and the people just getting more and more sensitive about political topics, no one could openly express their political opinion is no surprise to me but it just got worse. Economic wise the inflation is insane, business shutting down or met its maximum capacity because just too many people are in the same field, and I don't think this is a good sign for any country. I've been following all the crazy shit that is going on in the recent two months and I just couldn't imagine where this country is heading toward anymore.


I used to dreamed how China would rise and become better, more open, more free and all positive, but now I don't know anymore. There's really not that much of gap between nationalism and totalitarianism or even fascism. I hate to see that China would become like that but just feel powerless to do anything or to say anything because I know it wouldn't matter. You can't wake up people that are pretending to sleep and that is the reality in China. People who understand things would remain silence or being forced to be silence, and there are people who just don't understand and being manipulated by the media. It's really hard to dodge that trap of propaganda when you are exposed to all the them every day. I know that for fact how efficient they can be because it almost get myself influenced, all the slogans and patriotic videos you can find on Bilibili and other social media platforms, it's just everywhere.


I, too, found the country is shifting, and the direction of this time? I don't know or maybe I don't even dare to imagine. I love the country but just so little that I could do for her.

author: @donknowles2531
text:
I spent a year in China (Dalian, Changchun and Shenyang) in 2002.  My first trip to Beijing was in 1997, so I also saw a lot of the progress between those times and into, say, 2019 which was the last time I visited.  

And I visited several times in between, mostly Beijing, but other places as well, usually by train.

I also saw the "ghost towns" and have seen how quickly even 10yo buildings in Beijing have so quickly deterioriated, so I know about that from personal experience.  I remember seeing a lot of empty buildings out in Lijiang around 2016 or so when I visited there and wonder what has happened to them.  I suspect they are nearly in ruins, so that is probably a very common problem.

But, I do not think the Chinese "racism" against foreigners is anything new, especially when it comes to westerners with Chinese women.  The women I would be in public with (typically teachers) were often nervous even in 2002 and would be called prostitutes by the (usually "lower class") men who passed by.

And given the obvious alcohol abuse problems in China, it doesn't surprise me since about half of the men are 3 sheets to the wind most of the time in public, especially restaurants.  Particularly (but not exclusively) the lower class men.

I understood that even something as innocent as grabbing lunch nearby was a real problem for them, so just stopped even suggesting such things.  This seemed to vary from place to place (Changchun was much worse than Beijing or even Shenyang in this regard...) but, still...

Other than that, I also saw a good number of westerners who just did not seem to EVER understand that they were in a different country and that their behavior was not anywhere near normal or acceptable.  

I'm an "older" person so tended to get a pass on this.  But younger guys, in particular, seemed to have more issues with this.  Even the western women behaved in ways which were clearly outrageous by typical Chinese standards (at least to me).  

I was often surprised that we were tolerated as well as we were.  Perhaps the Chinese are just getting tired of watching things go "down the tubes" from their perspective with all the "foreign" influence.  Which could be anything from westerners to Kpop.  I can halfway understand their concern, though, even if it doesn't fit in with western thinking. 

Or maybe it's actually something much worse and oppressive.  Maybe they are taking a hard turn to the right and oppression.  Can't say I've been there enough lately to tell.

Anyway, it's an interesting perspective and I'm always open to new information since I don't go there as often as I have.

My understanding now (as in November 2021...), though, is that there IS definitely something going on with the local population.  A lot more anxiety and concern about potential Covid lockdowns or something on the horizon.  

Not exactly sure what, but certainly worth watching.

That said, I tend to take a lot of personal experiences in China with a grain of salt, because I know that sometimes people do things which bring attention to themselves.  I tend to not do that by nature, so my experiences are likely to be different from that of someone in their 20s or 30s...

author: @grunkle-g.2934
text:
I must say, thank you for not acting like the Z-A Megas are "worse" or "less inspired" than the ones that came before. They all follow the same design philosophy, some things really never change. But let's try to run the defense force on some of these guys. One important thing to note about every single Mega is the X/Y Mega Theory, which posits that every single Mega Evolution has letter theming incorporated into the design. Vast majority of the time it's either just an "X" or just a "Y", for a lot of legendaries/mythicals it's both, Rayquaza has delta, the Z Megas are Z plus the opposite letter of the OG, Zygarde is X/Y/Z. So with this in mind
- Aero's goatee and rock horns resemble a "Y".
- Mewtwo Y's head-tail combined with the horns resemble a "Y".
- Swampert when viewed from above and behind resembles a "Y" with its arms and torso.
- No matter where you view Gyarados from, it's a "Y". For example, from the front, its big fins plus its gaping maw.
- Mence's monowing alongside its tail makes it resemble a "Y".
- Excadrill has the three big drill points sticking out, akin to the three points of a "Y".
- Aggron's pointed chin and horns, that's another "Y".
- Scizor is our first "X" here. The pincers when opened up resemble an "X" from the right angle, as do its legs combined with its wings.
- They really hit you over the head with the "X" and "Y" theming on the Raichu Megas.
- Heracross is another "Y". The head horn plus its arms, then the eyebrows plus the nose horn.
- When Manectric roars, look at it from the front. The horns plus the bottom lightning bit, it's a "Y".
- Meganium is an "X" and quite the clever one. Without the neck flowers, it would very much resemble a "Y" with the neck plus antennae. However, the flower breaks that "Y" resemblence, as well as still making it resemble an "X" at certain places when combined with the antennae.
- Dragonite's head wings resembles a "Y" when combined with the tail.
- Feraligatr's hood sticking up plus the arm spikes, that's a "Y".
- Golisopod's extra arms resemble a "Y" when looking at it with its torso. As does the long beard plus the eyebrows.
- Blastoise's three cannons, that's another Excadrill situation, it's a "Y".
- Mega Glalie's head spikes and jaw spikes, that's an "X".

Next, some of the origins of the Megas
- Mewtwo Y actually resembles the original Mew, with all the smaller features and smaller body.
- Mega Swampert is just more Swampert. It always had swamp monster and sumo wrestler vibes.
- Gyarados may actually be an anime reference, resembling the "legendary Water Pokemon" Misty sees at one point.
- Mence's wing makes it resemble a fighter jet, a hang glider, and a blood moon.
- Aggron much more strongly resembles its pre-evolutions in its Mega. The rounder shapes plus it being more hunched over.
- Scovillain has always had the theming of being a Wild West gunslinger, and the Mega adds to that by making it resemble the common Western trope of the guys in black suits and ties. Might even be a "cowboys and Native Americans" thing going on with the red one's mohawk crest and the green one's wider seeds looking a bit more hatlike.
- Camerupt's "skirt" both resembles yak hair, and makes it look more like a massive volcano with the added fur being the rest of the hill.
- Mega Heracross is a Hercules beetle.
- Chomp Z is a play on Garchomp being a landshark. Now it's an airshark. Losing the Ground-type was so that bro wouldn't be busted with that stat spread.
- Gatr has a whole slew of origins, but, the one I think points strongest to the upward hood is the Drac. A mythological French dragon that lives in water, ambushes people on the riverside, and doesn't too strongly resemble a dragon. Already a strong fit for Mega Gatr. Then the Drac also has the ability to either shapeshift or turn invisible based on the story. Just so happens that Mega Feraligatr very much shifts its shape when making the Totodile head, as well as making its making its true appearance functionally invisible.
- Golisopod is a cyborg. Metal armor, extra attachments that also resemble shoulder cannons, really looks a lot like different sci-fi machines.

author: @ch-animatestudios
text:
I think it's the same-ness in the shapes. There's a lack of difference in character proportions and the shapes used. Using Wall-E as an example, Wall-E is a box. Squares are sturdy, safe shapes. Now look at EVE. EVE is a teardrop (basically a circle with a triangle). This shape, as well as the textures, implies higher tech, speed, and grace, as opposed to Wall-E's sturdy box. 

The Incredibles does this too. Mr. Incredible is a big, boxy character. It implies strength, stability. Dash is more triangular, implying speed, Edna has circles and complex shapes, implying sophistication. Syndrome is sharp, implying danger, and his Omnidroid is a sphere with sharp coming out (it's basically just an octopus). Toy Story, woody's got the hat and he's a cowboy, instantly recognizable, while Buzz is rounder and yet also a square, more future-y and implying action hero.

These newer movies, while not bad animation wise, are all same-y in terms of character design. It's all round, play-dough-y, and similar proportions. Not to say they're bad movies, just less iconic character designs. That's my current thoughts, I have more to say about character design (including color schemes, proportion, and silhouette), just not in YouTube comments.

text: I don't think it's fair to say pixar is adopting this "style" when it's just present in three movies out a whole roster. I don't even think it's fair to call this a style when it's just one design trait, I'd actually argue Luca and Turning Red have very different art direction (can't speak for Elio as I haven't watched it). One think you could sort of criticise is how their movies are very focused on child protagonists and narratives about childhood as of today, but even that is reductive: first because these are first and foremost children's movies, second because they don't paint a singular unified childhood experience (they deal with very different themes and subtexts) and then because every single person has been a child and therefore can find something to relate to in these narratives. Furthermore, the bean mouth is probably a symptom of the state of the industry as a whole, as it's a very simplified design that is probably easy and cheap to animate for studios trying to do their best with relative little support; it's also universal and accesible for audiences which makes me think the direction probably comes more from executives rather than artists, for the most part.

author: @buddhathegod
text:
Kinda disagree. If I'm being honest, while I love Up, Wall-E, Incredibles, Coco, etc, I was kind of feeling "3D pixar"-fatigue. The biggest issue for me is that it just felt so apparent that it was "locked inside 3D". That itself is not an issue, it's just that the volume of Pixar movies and then everyone who wanted follow suit had this look to it, how to train your dragon, etc. At the end of the day the animation was a bit limited to blendshapes, you could stretch and make some special frames but it was still in the realm of what we expected of 3D.

Weird sidestory: when I was growing up, my parents always wanted to accomodate me because I wasn't eating much. As soon as I said "yeah I like chicken nuggets", they'd make me chicken nuggets every day. And even though chicken nuggets are amazing, eventually I was growing tired of them. And it's kind of like what I feel like the industry is doing whenever they see positive sales numbers: they just force-feed us the same thing hoping it'll have the same result as that one first time.

At this time, I felt like I just wanted to see something new. It was almost like I was seeing the same artist's artstyle replicated over and over again, I wanted to see another artist's vision come to life in 3D. I'm sure there are other examples but I remember seeing "GuiltyGearXrd's Art Style" and the developers going through how they created frames and blended between techniques from 2D and 3D to get their results, talking about "adding in the imperfections of 2D" to achieve its style. This was telling me that it was possible to get other 2D artists styles into 3D, it was just a matter of will.

That's why I personally loved Luca.

It was a fun movie, a brand new style, and it had dipped into what was at this point quite rare: it broke conventional pixar 3D rigs. We had eyes on the same side of the face, mouths sliding side to side: it was just so refreshing to see a new artist's vision come to life. Then we had Spiderman: again, wonderful to see yet another artist's vision come to life, with snapping animation and visual effects of comic books. We got Arcane. And then we got... Luca's artstyle.... again... and then we got it... another time. 

For me the "Luca"-artstyle isn't the problem. The "Toy Story"-artstyle isn't the problem, nor is it upreme. The problem, to me, is that I think every artstyle is in itself integral to the storytelling. But the art gets commodified, it gets bottled up in this generic little flask that's suppoed to be "palpable to everyone" but then in the end just feels like it doesn't reach anyone. We have now seen that we have to ability to bring a lot of different artstyles to life, so why don't we?

Two notes:
- Treasure Planet was a timeless epic of animation, but flopped EXCLUSIVELY because of marketing drama
- Dreamworks' Bad Guys has "Bean Mouth" for a lot of background characters, and the "comic book" style reaction animation, and it still works - but main characters still have unique designs. Worth inspecting.
- I really think the shift is *intentional*. Less iconic designs mean more people can relate to the characters, larger viewing audience, etc. Also, and I think this is the most important thing: by PURPOSEFULLY using the same specific design language as previously established movies, viewers can know at a glance exactly what type of mood and tone the movie will have. Anybody traumatized by ANTZ when their mom was supposed to get A Bugs Life knows how setting a design apart can make a difference. Bean mouth = unmistakably safe for kids. In UP, the main character commits assault and battery and makes an innocent person BLEED. In Wall-E, huge existential societal problems are being exposed and commentated on. In Toy Story 4, we're forced to watch all the main characters contemplate certain death for a REALLY LONG TIME. Heck, in Toy Story 1 we see a character literally blown to smitherines by an effectively godlike character early on in the movie.

Those movies WERE made for all ages. Bean mouth is meant ONLY for kids. And that's okay, because kids need safety right now more than ever. Bean mouth = safety.

Most of the work of bank tellers is being pushed onto mobile apps in hopes that retail banks can buy and operate fewer buildings in general.

I am an IT engineer, and I've always been interested in technology since I was little (and I'm a 90s kid).I predicted this a decade or more ago. I was the last of my group of friends to acquire a smartphone, they couldn't believe it. Even though the idea of Android (the original idea of a Linux system - created by Google, back when Google was cool- running on a phone) excited me.
 I rejected how it was presented to the world, because I knew that instead of educating us in technology, the "business oriented" model would be based on the "dumb user" in which companies would take control, literally, of their technology and, thus, their lives, instead of companies relying in "user oriented" business models.
And that's exactly what's happening today. You've described it perfectly with all your examples. 
The solution lies in educating ourselves about technology. Knowing what we want, knowing what to avoid, and always being wary. The importance of self-criticism in order to choose a product instead of falling for the convictions of advertising and marketing. It is key to avoid surrounding ourselves with basic technology that, instead of solving our problems, creates new ones. Don't fall for advertising slogans. Filter based on what you really need and what you don't.

author: @FordGryph
text:
God I feel this entire video so goddamn much. 

My best example is how my work place handles how you do a “Leave of Absence” or in a broader sense “I literally cannot go to work because I am injured/ill or physically cannot make it, but lack the time off to do it without repercussions and you can’t make me work” type of situation.

See, I had gotten sick with COVID due to my sister being exposed to it at her own workplace meaning it was not only unsafe for me to go to work, but unsafe for my coworkers and the customers as well. 

This was well after the time where COVID was being taken seriously and they no longer gave any leniency for it, meaning if you had it you needed to have the sick time necessary or you’d get punished for staying home.

Unfortunately I lacked said time, and was forced to take a leave of absence. UNFORTUNATELY rather than simply giving me the time IN SPITE OF HAVING A DR’S NOTE TELLING THEM I HAD COVID AND TO STAY HOME, that wasn’t enough for them. I had to go through a third party website. 

The website was horribly confusing and made no sense, every number I was given to call was simply the same goddamn robot that didn’t help in the slightest and had no info on how to talk to a person. And when I FINALLY figured out how to do the thing I needed and finally spoke to an actual human, I thought it was over and I was going to be fine.

NOPE! Even after providing my dr’s note, proof that I went to the doctor a second time to check in, had them fax and email all my info to them, IT STILL WASN’T ENOUGH! 

They told me I had to provide some kind of information that I received treatment for my illness. Treatment… for COVID? WHA?? There IS NO treatment for COVID! I told them this and their best response was “lol idk figure it out.”

After that, I sat and thought for a moment, coughed my brains out, and said “yeah, f•ck this.” And just took the L and ate 2 absent points on my attendance since you are allowed 5 of them before you get fired.

What happened to the days where I could just show my boss a doctors note and he or she would be like “Hmm. Yup alright! Stay home get some rest, see you in a week!” Now I have to jump through flaming hoops while singing the national anthem in Japanese only for them to basically tell me to go F myself and eat two points anyway.
